The paper that matters most for the Marine heatwave early warning project is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

Here's why it stands out from the rest of the slate:

**It's the only paper that closes the loop from forecast to action.** The others are about building or evaluating forecasts; #4 shows what happens *after* a forecast — an expert workshop used an El Niño forecast to flag a severe marine heatwave risk, which triggered a pre-emptive rescue of 25 red handfish before the 2023/2024 event hit. That's the "early warning" part of your project name made concrete: a forecast that actually changes what people do.

**It's a worked example of the decision framework you'd need.** The paper walks through the whole chain — forecast signal, expert risk assessment, approvals, intervention, and post-release survival confirmation. For a project building an early warning system, that's a template for how to structure the "so what" end of the pipeline, not just the "here's the prediction" end.

**It's timely and directly on-topic.** It's new on the slate (entered 2026-11-10), it's about marine heatwaves specifically, and it's from 2026 — the same year as your project's active work.

The runner-up is **#5** (Mojumder, 2026), which evaluates 1–14-day ML forecasts of marine heatwaves against persistence benchmarks — directly relevant to the forecasting methodology side. But #4 is the one that speaks to the *purpose* of an early warning system, not just its mechanics.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for a high-resolution, four-dimensional temperature climatology for Northern Chilean Patagonia to provide reference conditions for detecting anomalies, assessing ecosystem functioning, and identifying long-term trends in a region with complex fjords and channels where satellite observation…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Reconstruction of temperature fields using the Data Interpolating Variational Analysis (DIVAnd) tool from approximately three million in situ observations collected over 75 years, producing monthly fields from the surface to 400 m depth with a horizontal resolution of about 900 m and over 32 vertic…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northern Chilean Patagonia, including specific features such as Reloncaví Sound, Comau and Puyuhuapi Fjords, Corcovado Gulf, and Ancud Gulf, based on in situ data collected over the past 75 years.
Abstract:
Abstract. Ocean climatologies are essential for understanding the mean state and variability of marine systems, providing reference conditions for detecting anomalies, assessing ecosystem functioning and identifying long-term trends. In this study, we present the first high-resolution, four-dimensional temperature climatology for Northern Chilean Patagonia, a region characterised by the presence of a complex network of fjords and channels. The climatology was generated from approximately three million in situ observations collected over the past 75 years from multiple datasets. Using the Data Interpolating Variational Analysis (DIVAnd) tool, temperature fields were reconstructed with a horizontal resolution of about 900 m and over 32 vertical levels, producing monthly fields from the surface to 400 m depth. The resulting climatology accurately reproduces the main spatial and seasonal temperature patterns reported in previous studies. Surface temperatures show strong summer gradients between the open Pacific and Northern Patagonia, while enclosed regions such as Reloncaví Sound, Comau and Puyuhuapi Fjords exhibit pronounced seasonal amplitude compared with the more stable Corcovado Gulf. Below surface, temperature gradients become smoother and the thermocline deepens in summer, typically ranging between 10 and 50 m. At 100 m depth, temperatures are relatively constant throughout the year, but spatial variations are still observed, with Ancud Gulf and Reloncaví Sound being slightly warmer. This climatology provides a refined and physically consistent representation of the oceanographic structure of Northern Patagonia, offering an essential baseline for future modelling, monitoring and climate-change assessments in a region where satellite observations are limited by persistent cloud cover and complex topography. All climatologies generated in this study are freely available online.

Here's the comparison:

**#1 – GOOS (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)**
This is about strengthening the *infrastructure* of global ocean observation: deploying equipment, running observing system experiments, network optimization, and co-creating technology roadmaps with industry. The focus is on closing structural gaps in under-observed regions (deep sea, polar) and ensuring continuity of the GOOS framework under IOC-UNESCO. It's a big, systems-level call — think "keep the global observing network alive and open."

**#2 – Antarctica & Southern Ocean (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)**
This is a *research* call: resolving uncertainties in Southern Ocean and Antarctic projections, understanding ocean–ice–atmosphere interactions, improving Earth System Models and regional coupled models, and developing monitoring indicators. It explicitly calls for work on extreme events, tipping elements, and decadal-to-millennial projections.

**Which fits the Marine heatwave early warning project better?**

**#2 is the stronger fit.** Here's why:

- Your project is about *forecasting* marine heatwaves — building and evaluating prediction methods (your slate includes ML forecast evaluation #8, a forecast-triggered response strategy #7, and a regional ocean forecast system analysis #13). #2 explicitly asks for improving projections, reducing uncertainties in extreme events, and enhancing Earth System Models and regional coupled models. That's the same intellectual territory.
- #1 is more about the *observing infrastructure* itself — deploying sensors, optimizing networks, governance. While your project certainly *uses* observations, its core contribution is on the prediction/forecasting side, not on building the observing system.
- #2's scope on "extreme events and mid-latitude weather" and "abrupt, irreversible change/tipping elements" maps directly onto marine heatwave prediction.

**One caveat:** #2 is geographically scoped to Antarctica and the Southern Ocean. If your project's heatwave work is in other regions (e.g., the Bay of Bengal, as in #8), you'd need to frame the contribution in terms of Southern Ocean relevance or as a methodological advance that applies there. #1 is geographically broader (global, with emphasis on areas beyond national jurisdiction), so it's easier to fit any region — but the infrastructure focus is a harder mismatch.

**Bottom line:** If your heatwave work has a Southern Ocean angle or you can frame the forecasting methods as applicable to that region, go with #2. If the work is firmly in a different basin and you want a broader geographic fit, #1 is the fallback — but you'd be pitching an observing-infrastructure story that may not be your project's strength.

## Best-fitting open grant: #4 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System

Of the ten open grants on the project's slate, **#4** is the strongest fit for the Marine heatwave early warning project (#1).

**Why it fits:** The project's core is ML-based ocean data assimilation feeding SST/heatwave forecasting, and #4 is explicitly about strengthening and operationalising the global ocean observing system — the observation backbone that a heatwave early-warning system depends on. The call's own reading names "observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs)" and "network optimisation" as methods, which is exactly the data-assimilation/forecasting work the project does. It's a large call (€50M) and still open, with a deadline of **2027-02-16**.

**The biggest doubt:** #4 is framed around *biodiversity and ecosystem* observations and areas beyond national jurisdiction, whereas the project is a physical-oceanography/forecasting effort. You'd be pitching a heatwave-prediction capability into a call whose headline outcomes are biodiversity and EU strategic autonomy — so the proposal needs to make the observing-system/forecasting link explicit rather than assume it.

The runner-up, **#7** (Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity, €3–8M, deadline 2027-09-22), is a closer methodological match on the remote-sensing + AI side, but it is biodiversity-centric and its slots (omics, in-situ biodiversity frameworks) are mostly gaps for this lab. **#3** (NSF OTIC) is the weakest fit — it's about instrumentation development, and no lab member's profile covers that slot.

## Who in the lab should lead

**You (Mara Ellison)** should lead, with **Priya Raman (#16)** as the natural co-lead.

- **You** cover the call's central slot — "stabilise, strengthen and operationalise the global ocean observing system" — on the strength of your declared ocean-data-assimilation work, which is the project's method. That's the strongest single claim in the lab for #4.
- **Priya (#16)** covers the same slot from the satellite-remote-sensing side, and the nightly ranking named her first for #4. Her satellite ocean-colour work is the observing-side complement to your assimilation/forecasting lead.

The project's three members (you, Tomás, Sun-hee) all map to the project's concepts, but for *this call* the two strongest declared-profile matches are you and Priya. Tomás (#18, physics-informed ML) and Sun-hee (#17, ocean data tools) are useful supporting members — Tomás on the ML/forecasting method, Sun-hee on the data-tooling/delivery side — but neither is a declared fit for #4's core slot.

**Gaps to fill for #4:** no one in the lab covers observing-system experiments (OSEs), OSSEs, network optimisation, or areas beyond national jurisdiction, and the call asks for an **industry** partner. Those are the slots you'd need to close with a partner or a reframing of the proposal.

   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.

1. Read the call (`corpus_item`). Then `knowledge_people_for_call`, which
   returns, per person, the requirement slots they cover and the evidence tier
   of each: **declared** (they said so in their profile), **demonstrated**
   (their own papers), **confirmed in conversation** (they told Mylo and said
   yes when asked).
2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when
   collaborator search is on and people consented; never speculate beyond them.
4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you
   cannot see.

- enhanced collaboration between observation communities, marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators, actionably contributing to the validation, procurement readiness, uptake and large-scale deployment of innovative ocean observing technologies and approaches, in particular for biodiversity observations, while reinforcing the long-term sustainability of the global ocean observing system.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

Here's what I found, and where I got cut off.

## Best-fitting open grant

The Plastic pathways slate (#8) has two open grants:

- **#9 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System** (Horizon Europe, €50M, deadline 2027-02-16). Focuses on strengthening GOOS: deploying observation equipment, observing-system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), network optimisation, and closing structural gaps in under-observed regions (deep sea, polar, areas beyond national jurisdiction).
- **#16 — Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination** (NSF OTIC, deadline 2027-02-15). Supports instrumentation development with broad applicability to ocean science.

**#9 is the better fit for Plastic pathways.** The project's core work — Lagrangian particle tracking of marine litter, observation-grounded transport and beaching modelling, and satellite-based detection — maps directly onto GOOS's call for observation networks, data delivery, and closing gaps in under-observed regions. The project's slate papers (#13, #20, #24) are all about observation-grounded plastic transport, which is exactly the kind of "critical observations for marine biodiversity and ecosystem knowledge" that #9 asks for. #16 is more about building new instruments, which is a narrower and less direct match.

## Who in the lab should lead

Mylo's nightly ranking named two people for #9:

- **#4 Priya Raman** — satellite ocean remote sensing; her work on mapping water quality from space contributes directly to strengthened observing capacities and data coordination.
- **#2 You (Mara Ellison)** — data assimilation with ML for ocean forecasting; your work enhances the resilience and accuracy of observing-system outputs.

**Priya should lead the application.** Her declared satellite oceanography is the closest single match to GOOS's emphasis on observation networks and data delivery, and she's a project member. You would be the natural co-lead, bringing the data-assimilation and forecasting angle that GOOS's "reliable services" and Copernicus Marine Service threads need. Jonah (#3) is the third project member and the lab's marine-litter/Lagrangian specialist — he'd be the domain lead on the plastic-pathways science itself.

## Who outside the lab could partner

I was able to identify several strong external candidates from the corpus, but **I ran out of steps before I could check co-authorship paths or confirm introductions for all of them.** Here's what I found:

- **Santiago Bravo, Eugenia Pasanisi, Svitlana Liubartseva, Giovanni Coppini** (#24) — Mediterranean Lagrangian particle tracking of floating macro-litter, using Parcels and Copernicus Marine Service reanalysis. Very close methodological match to the project.
- **Amemou, Hilaire, Cecchi, Philippe, Koné, Vamara, Penven, Pierrick, Lett, Christophe** (#20) — Lagrangian particle tracking (Ichthyop) of urban plastic dispersal and beaching along the Côte d'Ivoire coast, forced by CROCO. Directly relevant to plastic pathways.
- **Sehan Lim, Sunwook Hong** (#13) — tide-resolving beaching kernel for OceanParcels, applied to field records from Uido, Korea. Same particle-tracking toolkit.
- **Wang, Yanyun, Ye, Xin, Cheng, Dongdong, et al.** (#26) — submarine groundwater discharge as a microplastic input pathway to the coastal ocean. Adds a source-side angle.
- **Takuro Uehara, Mateo Cordier, Laurent Lebreton** (#21) — system dynamics model of global plastic transport, degradation, and cleanup to 2050. Brings the global-scale and policy angle.
- **Valeria Teso, Diego Urteaga, et al.** (#23) — ROV survey of deep-sea marine litter in the Mar del Plata Submarine Canyon. Addresses the "deep sea" gap that #9 explicitly calls out.
- **A. Brilke, Martina Calovi, Jan Ketil Rød, Isabel Richter** (#25) — regional differences in plastic accumulation along the Norwegian coast. Adds a northern-European coastal perspective.

**What I could not finish:** I did not get to run `knowledge_introduction_paths` on these external authors to see if there are warm co-authorship chains from your lab to any of them, nor did I check whether any of them are in labs or departments you can already see. That would tell you which of these partners are realistically reachable versus which would need a cold outreach. If you'd like, I can do that as a next step.

#24 [paper] Marine litter in the Mediterranean: observation-based Lagrangian particle tracking
Authors: Santiago Bravo, Eugenia Pasanisi, Svitlana Liubartseva, Giovanni Coppini, Alice Madonia, Igor Atake, Marta Azzolin, Lara Carosso
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1936698
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of spatially explicit, observation-grounded predictions for the transport and coastal deposition of floating marine macro-litter (FMML) in the Mediterranean.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework using Parcels, initialized with monthly gridded FMML observations from shipboard surveys and forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusio…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean Sea, specifically areas surveyed via the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries from August 2023 to December 2024.
Abstract:
Introduction The Mediterranean is a major hotspot for floating marine macro-litter (FMML) accumulation, yet spatially explicit, observation-grounded predictions of its transport and coastal deposition remain scarce. We present a data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework that uses monthly gridded FMML observations from systematic shipboard surveys as simulation initial conditions complementing existing source-based modelling approaches. Methods Observations were collected from August 2023 to December 2024 within the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries as monitoring platforms under a standardised protocol. A total of 158 surveys detected 4,801 FMML items across approximately 6,200 km² of surveyed sea surface, of which more than 62% were artificial polymers. Observed monthly FMML item counts at 5 × 5 km resolution initialised ensemble Lagrangian simulations (18 members per target month; 17.2–32.5 million virtual particles per seeding window, 5,000 particles per observed item) using Parcels, forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusion scheme. Monthly frequency-of-occurrence maps were computed at the sea surface and on coastlines. Results The Southern Tyrrhenian and Northern Ligurian seas, including the Pelagos Sanctuary, exhibited in 2024 near-persistent high sea surface FMML occurrence, peaking in late summer–autumn and reaching a seasonal minimum in winter–early spring. The Balearic Sea showed elevated occurrence from late spring through summer (May–September), declining through autumn. The Adriatic displayed intense sub-basin-scale spreading from January to June and again in December, with summer leakage into the Northern Ionian Sea. Coastal deposition frequencies were highest on Corsica, western Sardinia and northern Tunisia, then the south-eastern Tyrrhenian and Ligurian–Tuscan margins, with Valencia–Barcelona largely confined to summer. Integration with loggerhead turtle nesting records illustrates how coastal frequency-of-occurrence maps can support conservation applications. Discussion A web-based Particle Analysis Dashboard translates these outputs into an interactive tool with Marine Protected and Conserved Area overlays for scientists and decision-makers. The framework provides a scalable, observation-anchored foundation for MSFD Descriptor 10 monitoring, transferable to other semi-enclosed sea basins. Priority future work includes complementary validation against independent beach-litter monitoring data, integration of land-based source inventories, and linkage with species distribution models.

#20 [paper] Modeling dispersal and beaching of urban plastic waste along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire.
Authors: Amemou, Hilaire, Cecchi, Philippe, Koné, Vamara, Penven, Pierrick, Lett, Christophe
Venue: Marine pollution bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42735662/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The processes governing the fate, dispersal, and coastal retention of urban plastic debris along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, which is vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO) to simulate the dispersal and beaching of plastic particles.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, specifically focusing on the region around Abidjan and the broader Ivorian coast.
Abstract:
Plastic pollution is a growing concern in West Africa's marine environment, yet the processes governing its fate remain poorly understood. The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire is particularly vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs from rivers and lagoons. This study investigates the dispersal and coastal retention of urban plastic debris using a Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO). We provide the first regional-scale assessment of seasonal beaching dynamics along the Ivorian coast using a high-resolution coupled hydrodynamic-Lagrangian framework. Simulations show that while a large fraction of particles is transported offshore (~52%), a substantial proportion (~48%) remains nearshore and beaches at least once. Persistent accumulation hotspots are identified around Abidjan, regardless of the release location. Seasonal variability strongly controls debris pathways. During the minor upwelling season (January-April), beaching occurs predominantly west of Abidjan, associated with weaker currents and enhanced coastal retention. In contrast, during the major upwelling season (June-September), intensified currents and mesoscale activity promote wider dispersal and shift beaching eastward. From October to December, beaching intensifies along the eastern coastline. These results highlight the dominant role of regional hydrodynamics in shaping marine debris distribution and demonstrate the value of high-resolution Lagrangian modeling for identifying pollution hotspots and supporting mitigation strategies in data-scarce coastal regions.

#26 [paper] Submarine groundwater discharge: An overlooked but quantifiable pathway for microplastics inputs to the coastal ocean.
Authors: Wang, Yanyun, Ye, Xin, Cheng, Dongdong, Cui, Shouxin, Qian, Weixu, Pan, Feng, Zhang, Yuanjing, Li, Yasong
Venue: Journal of environmental management
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42868812/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine microplastics (MPs) pollution has become a serious concern, in which submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) is an overlooked yet potentially significant pathway for land-based MPs entering the ocean. This study examined the occurrence, correlated factors, and SGD-derived flux of MPs in the groundwater of a representative coastal city in China. MPs were widely detected in groundwater at relatively low levels, with an average abundance of 2.4 ± 1.0 n/L, and exhibited distinct physicochemical characteristics. Fibers represented the most abundant morphological types, while transparent and black particles were the predominant colors. Over half of the MPs were less than 500 μm in size. MPs occurrence was primarily governed by hydrological season (dry > wet), functional zone (estuarine > transitional > urban), and well type (open > covered), reflecting the combined effects of dilution, pollution sources, land use, and input pathways. Based on a radium isotope (226Ra) mass-balance model, the total SGD flux was estimated at 4.0 × 107 m3/d, of which the freshwater component constituted 3.3 × 106 m3/d. We conservatively estimated that fresh SGD carried (2.6 ± 0.4) × 1012 microplastic particles (2.6 ± 0.5 tons) into coastal waters annually, accounting for approximately 11.3% ± 6.0% of the total riverine MPs flux into Xiamen Bay. These findings confirm that SGD constitutes a non-negligible pathway for land-based microplastics, highlighting the necessity of incorporating groundwater transport into coastal plastic pollution assessment and management strategies.

#25 [paper] Uncovering regional differences in plastic pollution distribution along the Norwegian coast
Authors: A. Brilke, Martina Calovi, Jan Ketil Rød, Isabel Richter
Venue: International Journal of Environmental Science and Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s13762-026-07430-8
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding the mechanisms behind coastal plastic accumulation to enable targeted clean-up actions and policy-making.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Linear regression using plastic weight and item count as response variables against physical and socio-environmental explanatory variables.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 446 sampling transects across 170 beaches on Norway’s south-eastern, southern, western, and northern coasts.
Abstract:
Abstract Understanding the mechanisms behind coastal plastic accumulation is crucial for more targeted clean-up actions and policy-making. We used a systematically collected dataset for plastic pollution along the Norwegian coast, added physical and socio-environmental response variables to it, and used linear regression to identify the most important factors that influence plastic accumulation. We used 446 sampling transects on 170 beaches from Norway’s south-eastern, southern, western and northern coasts. Plastic weight and count were chosen as response variables in several linear models, with different explanatory variables included. Although the explained variance in plastic pollution did not lead to any meaningful insights regarding plastic distribution, other insights were gained. Measuring plastic pollution by weight or item count led to different correlations of predictor variables. There were significant regional differences in models, and some predictor variables clearly show different values depending on the region. Furthermore, geographical beaching patterns of different types of plastic debris along the Norwegian coast found in the literature were confirmed. The southern coast had the largest number of plastic items per sampling area, whilst the north displayed fewer but heavier items. Dividing the data by region seems to be desirable, but more samples per region are needed.

#22 [paper] Marine plastic pollution: ecological risks, environmental distribution, and sustainable mitigation perspectives
Authors: F. A. Samiul Islam
Venue: EQA - International Journal of Environmental Quality
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.60923/issn.2281-4485/25086
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine plastic pollution has become a major environmental challenge affecting marine biodiversity, ecosystem stability, environmental quality, and human well-being across coastal and oceanic ecosystems. Increasing plastic production, ineffective waste management, urbanization, and transboundary transport processes have accelerated the accumulation of macroplastics, microplastics, and nanoplastics in aquatic environments. This review critically evaluates the major sources, transport pathways, environmental distribution, ecological impacts, socio-economic implications, and mitigation strategies associated with marine plastic contamination. Plastic pollutants primarily originate from municipal waste discharge, riverine transport, fisheries, aquaculture, industrial activities, wastewater effluents, and maritime operations, followed by widespread redistribution through hydrodynamic and atmospheric processes. Major ecological consequences include entanglement, ghost fishing, ingestion, trophic transfer, oxidative stress, endocrine disruption, habitat degradation, pathogen dispersal, and biodiversity decline. Plastic contamination additionally threatens fisheries productivity, seafood safety, tourism economies, public health, and ecosystem-service sustainability. Current mitigation approaches increasingly emphasize circular-economy transition, extended producer responsibility, international governance frameworks, ecosystem-based management, and advanced environmental monitoring technologies. However, substantial challenges remain regarding policy implementation, recycling efficiency, technological inequality, and transboundary waste leakage. Integrated environmental governance, sustainable production systems, scientific monitoring, and evidence-based mitigation strategies are therefore essential for improving long-term marine environmental quality and reducing global plastic contamination.

Method (Mycelium's reading): A critical review evaluating state-of-the-art technologies across the marine plastics value chain, including remote sensing, robotic platforms, machine-vision systems, downstream sorting (electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging, AI-driven classification), and mechanic…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe
Abstract:
Marine Plastic Pollution (MPP) is widely recognised as a significant global challenge, driven by unsustainable plastic production, ineffective waste management, and the long-term persistence of plastics in marine environments. MPP has become increasingly widespread across oceans, along coastlines and on the seafloor, resulting in an urgent need for the development of technologies capable of advancing a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products. Advances in cleaner production technologies, including satellite and drone-based remote sensing, autonomous robotic platforms, and machine-vision systems, have improved the efficiency of plastic debris identification, classification, and recovery in complex marine environments. Similarly, innovations in downstream sorting, such as electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging (HSI), and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven classification, are enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of processing MPP. The review evaluates mechanical recycling methods with particular emphasis on recent advances in extrusion, moulding technologies, and additive manufacturing for converting MPP into high-value secondary materials in a CE framework in Europe. These technological developments demonstrate the potential for establishing viable and scalable valorisation routes. Overall, the review outlines key opportunities to strengthen a sustainable CE and guide future research and industrial adoption. In doing so, it provides a comprehensive examination of state-of-the-art technologies across the entire marine plastics value chain in Europe, from detection and recovery to separation, identification, and recycling.

#21 [paper] Halting marine plastic inputs by 2050 is necessary but not sufficient to avoid microplastic accumulation
Authors: Takuro Uehara, Mateo Cordier, Laurent Lebreton
Venue: Communications Earth & Environment
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-026-04054-1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine plastic pollution threatens ecosystems, economies, and human health, yet economic literature overlooks the transport of plastic debris across marine ecosystem compartments and its natural breakdown. Here we show, using a system dynamics model, the global physical and economic efforts required to remove buoyant marine plastic debris by 2050. The model simulates the degradation, transport, and cleanup of macroplastics and their breakdown into microplastics across shoreline, coastal, and offshore zones. Scenario analyses explore varying rates of waste input reduction and cleanup intensity. Results indicate that halting new marine plastic inputs by 2050, as outlined in the G20 Implementation Framework for Actions on Marine Plastic Litter, and removing existing buoyant macroplastics may be insufficient to prevent substantial microplastic accumulation. Accelerating cleanup efforts can reduce microplastic generation, albeit at a higher cost. Estimated annual cleanup expenses range from €0.1–5.6 billion, representing 0.3–15.7% of national pollution abatement budgets and 0.0001–0.0052% of global GDP. Stopping new marine plastic inputs and removing buoyant macroplastics by 2050 may still leave substantial microplastic accumulation, and rapid cleanup to reduce microplastic generation would cost 0.1–5.6 billion euros annually, according to a system dynamics model.

#19 [paper] Spatial Patterns of Marine Litter on a Remote South Atlantic Ocean Island: Setting Baselines for Monitoring
Authors: Fernanda Caminha Leal Valls, Leandro Bugoni
Venue: Thalassas An International Journal of Marine Sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s41208-026-01266-2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Characterizing the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter on Trindade Island, a remote South Atlantic island, to establish baselines for monitoring before the establishment of marine protected areas.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Systematic sampling of seven beaches with varying exposure to wind and substrate; quantification of litter items, categorization by purpose, and calculation of pollution indices (Clean Coast Index and Plastic Abundance Index).
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Seven beaches on Trindade Island, South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland; characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates.
Abstract:
Abstract Marine plastic litter is a major environmental problem across all oceans, including remote regions. Here, we described the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter stranded on the beaches of Trindade Island, in the South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland, before the establishment of marine protected areas and the initiation of a long-term research program on the island. Seven beaches differing in exposure to wind and substrate were sampled. A total of 1317 litter items were recorded, with plastics as the main litter (81.9%), mostly hard plastic fragments. Although Lixo Beach had the smallest surveyed area (425 m 2 ), it exhibited the highest litter density (0.74 items/m 2 ) and highest litter-covered area (2.2% of the sampled beach area). Domestic and household purpose items composed the bulk of identifiable items (28.9%), followed by naval (22.5%) and fishery (17.7%) pieces. Litter distribution among beaches differed, with leeward beaches accumulating significantly more and larger litter items than windward beaches, revealing substantial local-scale variation patterns in debris retention. These beaches are characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates rather than sand. Our analysis of pollution indices demonstrated that the Clean Coast Index ( CCI ) and the Plastic Abundance Index ( PAI ) are strongly correlated and suitable for long-term monitoring. This study confirms that oceanic islands are prone to accumulating marine litter, while contrasting results from other studies on Trindade Island emphasize the need for simple yet standardized protocols to support long-term monitoring of plastic pollution in remote environments.

#23 [paper] Out of sight, hidden into the deep: Marine litter in the Mar del Plata Submarine Canyon (southwestern Atlantic) revealed by ROV survey
Authors: Valeria Teso, Diego Urteaga, Graziella Bozzano, Gregório Bigatti, Martín Brogger, Francisco Brusa, Rodrigo Calderón, NADIA CERINO
Venue: PLoS ONE
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0357098
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The deep sea is increasingly recognized as vulnerable to anthropogenic pressures, including marine litter, yet large geographic gaps remain in our understanding of litter distribution and ecological interactions. Submarine canyon systems can act as conduits and accumulation zones for anthropogenic material, but data from the southwestern Atlantic are scarce. Here, we present the first characterization of deep-sea marine macro-litter in the Mar del Plata Submarine Canyon (Argentina), based on 240 hours of remotely operated vehicle (ROV) video collected during 17 dives (878-3,820 m depth) aboard the R/V Falkor (too) in July-August 2025. Litter was observed during 10 dives, comprising 29 items distributed between 1,120 and 3,820 m. Plastic was the dominant material (27 items), followed by rubber (2 items). Most litter consisted of plastic sheets and bags, food wrappers, and commercial fishing-related gear, including lines, ropes, and cables. Litter was observed in multiple settings, including buried or degraded items, resting on the seabed, and trapped among rocks or drifting near the bottom. Most items were located within the canyon domain, forming localized clusters along the canyon axis and walls. Litter-fauna interactions were documented for seven items and included both sessile colonization and associations with mobile fauna, mainly on partially buried plastic items and entangled fishing-related gear. These patterns suggest that substrate stability and residence time may influence sessile colonization. The composition and distribution of debris indicate that maritime activities, particularly fisheries, are the most likely sources and further support the role of submarine canyons as accumulation zones for marine litter. This study provides critical baseline data in an understudied region and highlights the need for improved monitoring programs and management strategies for marine litter to reduce impacts in submarine canyon systems.

#28 [paper] Cross-ecosystem assessment of macroplastic pollution in mangrove, coral reef, seagrass, and beach habitats of tropical small islands.
Authors: Yunanto, Agung, Wisha, Ulung Jantama, Romdon, Ahmad, Arifin, Zainal, Priyono, Bayu, Falahudin, Dede, Handayani, Tri, Ondara, Koko
Venue: Marine pollution bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42896361/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine plastic pollution poses an increasing threat to tropical coastal ecosystems; however, comparative understanding of macroplastic accumulation across interconnected habitats remains limited, particularly in small-island environments. This study assessed macroplastic density and composition across mangroves, coral reefs, seagrass meadows, and beaches on three tropical small islands (Panjang, Semujur, and Ketawai) in western Bangka, Indonesia. Field surveys were conducted in May 2025 using ecosystem-specific transect methods, and macroplastic debris was quantified in terms of abundance, weight, volume, and composition. Macroplastic accumulation exhibited clear habitat-dependent patterns. Across the three islands, beaches consistently recorded the highest debris densities (0.193 ± 0.0083-0.680 ± 0.0310 items/m2), whereas coral reefs exhibited the lowest densities (0.003 ± 0.0005-0.009 ± 0.0011 items/m2). Seagrass meadows showed generally low to moderate accumulation (0.002 ± 0.0003-0.082 ± 0.0102 items/m2), while mangroves exhibited intermediate densities (0.067 ± 0.0027 items/m2). Habitat-level differences were statistically significant (Kruskal-Wallis: χ2 = 78.9, p < 0.001), whereas total debris density did not differ significantly among islands. Food- and beverage-related plastics dominated beach and seagrass habitats, whereas coral reefs consisted exclusively of fishing-related debris. Hierarchical clustering and NMDS ordination (stress = 0.1084) consistently revealed stronger compositional structuring by habitat than by island. PERMANOVA further indicated that habitat accounted for a greater proportion of compositional variation than island identity (R2 = 0.465, p = 0.104). These findings demonstrate that macroplastic accumulation across tropical small islands is primarily structured by habitat characteristics and local retention processes, highlighting the need for habitat-specific mitigation measures and integrated coastal management.

#11 [paper] A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period.
Authors: Zhenhua Zhang, Peng Chen, Siqi Zhang, Delu Pan
Venue: Science Advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aej4633
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The authors used 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP). A bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions, and low-light estimates were generated as physically const…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Arctic region, specifically marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions, using spaceborne LiDAR data from 2006 to 2023.
Abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year −1 during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, plus the papers and funding opportunity I'd point at.

## Where the project stands

I can see the project is a lab-level effort with three members — Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you. However, I don't have a confirmed state for it: no recorded goals, method, stage, milestones, or open blockers are stored, and I can't see when it was last reviewed. So I can't tell you how far along it is or what's blocking it — if you'd like, you can update the project's state in the app and I'll be able to give a fuller review next time.

What I *can* tell you is that its slate is active: all ten items on it entered this week (2026-11-10 to 2026-11-13), so Mycelium is actively feeding it fresh material.

## Three most relevant new papers

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026). The closest match: a three-phase beaching kernel for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, with full code and aggregated results. If Plastic pathways involves particle tracking of debris to shore, this is directly reusable.

2. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026). Not about plastic, but a strong methodological template: a YOLO11-based detector for low-contrast, curved features in satellite imagery, with a decade of MODIS data. If any part of the project involves spotting debris or plumes from space, the detection/segmentation approach transfers well.

3. **#7 — "Comment on egusphere-2026-5844"** (2026). A seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific (MOM6 + SIS2 + COBALT, ~10 km resolution) with 32 years of retrospective forecasts. Relevant as a reference for how to build and evaluate a regional forecasting framework — useful if Plastic pathways couples debris transport to forecasted currents.

The other slate items (#4, #5, #9, #11) are further afield — Arctic phytoplankton, a Pacific forecast system analysis, multi-agent tracking, and biogeochemical-Argo — so I'd deprioritise them for this project.

## One funding opportunity

**#12 — "Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity, towards a fully interoperable observation and data framework"** (Horizon, €3M–€8M, deadline 2027-09-22, still open).

- **Why it fits:** the call asks for multisensory data-integration systems that harmonise in-situ observations with satellite remote sensing and AI analytics, with demonstration cases in marine ecosystems under pressure. Plastic pathways sits in the lab's "debris pathways" cluster, and the lab's stated method is combining ocean models, satellite observations and ML — so a proposal framing debris-pathway tracking as an in-situ + remote-sensing + AI integration case for a coastal ecosystem under pressure would land squarely in scope.
- **Biggest doubt:** the call is biodiversity-focused, so the debris angle needs to be framed in terms of ecosystem impact (e.g. pollution pressure on habitats under the Marine Strategy Framework Directive) rather than pure transport modelling. Also, I can't see the eligibility rules for your institution's country or the consortium requirements, so check those before committing.

The other grant on the slate, #8 (NSF OTIC), is about instrumentation development — a weaker fit unless the project is building new hardware. #3 (Global Ocean Observing System) is broader and more policy-oriented.

**Suggested next steps:** confirm the project's state in the app (goals, method, blockers) so I can tie the slate to specific blockers; and if #12 looks right, I can dig into its full text to check eligibility and draft a fit assessment.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

- develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. Proposals should take into account socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems, including land and sea use and emissions of pollutants (e.g. agriculture, aquaculture, urbanization, resource exploitation and management practices). Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

final_text:
The one that matters most is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, *Conservation Science and Practice*).

Why it stands out for the project:

- **It is the proof-of-concept your project is trying to build.** In January 2024, forecasts ahead of the 2023/24 El Niño flagged a high risk of marine heatwaves in Australia. An expert workshop judged the forecasted extremes (>20°C or ~+3°C) a severe threat, and that triggered a pre-emptive rescue: 25 red handfish were captured, held for three months, and released after the heatwave subsided, with post-release survival confirmed (#4, Abstract). That is exactly the chain your project wants to formalize — *forecast → risk assessment → early action* — demonstrated end-to-end in a real event.
- **It shows what "early warning" is for.** The paper frames the forecast not as an academic product but as the trigger for a concrete, time-critical decision that bought the species time during record temperatures (80 days more than 2°C above the long-term mean summer temperature, #4, Abstract). That's the value proposition you'll be making to managers and stakeholders.
- **It's recent and current** (2026, still open), so it's a live reference for how the conservation community is operationalizing MHW forecasts right now.

The runner-up is **#5** (1–14-day ML forecasts of MHWs in the Northern Bay of Bengal vs. persistence benchmarks), which is directly on your ML-for-MHW-forecasting interest, but it's a thesis data/code release with a thin abstract, so it's more of a methods reference than a strategic one. **#3** (seasonal Northeast Pacific ocean forecasting) is also relevant to the forecasting infrastructure side, but it's a comment on a preprint and broader than heatwaves.

If you'd like, I can pull the full text of #4 to dig into how the forecast-to-action decision was structured — that's the part most transferable to your early warning design.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

The clearest fit for Plastic pathways is **#4 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it stands out:

- **It is the only item on the slate squarely about marine litter.** The rest of the feed is phytoplankton production (#3, #9), ocean forecast model analyses (#5), internal wave detection (#7), turtle telemetry (#12), and other remote-sensing work — none of which touch debris pathways directly.
- **It is a methods paper with open code.** It ships a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, the experiment scripts, and the aggregated result files behind every number in the manuscript (#4). That is directly reusable: a beaching kernel is exactly the kind of component a pathways project needs to model where floating debris ends up on shore.
- **It is validated against field records.** The kernel was developed and tested against actual beaching observations from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories (#4) — so it is a worked example of the full chain from flow field to particle tracking to ground truth, which is the same chain your project follows.
- **It is fresh and open.** It entered the slate on 2026-11-10 and is still current (#4).

One caveat: I could not read the project's confirmed state (goals, method, blockers) in this conversation, so I am judging fit from the project's name and your lab's declared interest in debris pathways. If the team has a specific open blocker — say, a beaching or deposition model to validate — #4 is the item to pull first; the code and reproduction record make it the most actionable paper on the slate.

If you want, I can also read the full text of #4 to check exactly how the three-phase kernel handles tides, or check whether any other slate item speaks to a particular blocker the team has listed.

Here's the comparison.

**#1 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System** (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)
This call is about stabilising and expanding the *infrastructure* of global ocean observation: deploying equipment, running observing-system experiments, network optimisation, and technology roadmaps with industry. The emphasis is on closing structural gaps in under-observed regions (polar, deep sea, areas beyond national jurisdiction) and on EU strategic autonomy in observation capacity.

**#2 — Unlocking a safe operating space for Antarctica and the Southern Ocean** (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)
This call is about *understanding and projecting* the future of the Antarctic/Southern Ocean: ocean–atmosphere–sea-ice–ice-sheet interactions, improving Earth System Models and regional coupled models, monitoring indicators, and explicitly including **extreme events and mid-latitude weather** in its scope.

**Fit against the Marine heatwave early warning project (#3):**

The project's core is forecasting marine heatwaves — a prediction/forecasting problem, not an infrastructure-deployment problem.

- **#2 fits better.** Its scope explicitly calls for improving projections, reducing uncertainties in projected changes, and includes "extreme events" as a named target. A marine heatwave early-warning system is a projection/forecasting effort aimed at extreme events, which sits squarely in #2's aims. The method (improving ESMs and regional coupled models, monitoring indicators) also aligns with what a heatwave forecasting project would need.

- **#1 is a weaker fit.** It is fundamentally about the observing *system* — hardware, networks, governance, and EU strategic autonomy. While a heatwave early-warning project would *use* observations, the call's expected outcomes are about deploying equipment and strengthening GOOS governance, not about building or evaluating forecasting methods. The project would be a consumer of what #1 funds, not the thing #1 is asking for.

**Biggest doubt on #2:** the call is geographically anchored to Antarctica and the Southern Ocean. If the project's heatwave work is focused on other regions (e.g., temperate or tropical coasts), the geographic scope is a real constraint. I could not see the project's detailed problem statement or milestones in this conversation, so I can't confirm whether the project's target region overlaps with the Southern Ocean.

**What I could not check:** the project's full problem statement, method, and milestones (the project detail was not visible to me here), and the full eligibility rules of either call (institution type, consortium requirements, etc.). If the project's focus is outside the Southern Ocean, #2's geographic scope would be the deciding factor against it.

final_text:
Here's what I found, in three parts.

---

## 1. Best-fitting open grant

**#1 — "Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate"** (Horizon CL5-2027-01-D1-07, €3M–€15M, deadline **4 March 2027**, still open).

This is the strongest match for the Marine heatwave early warning project (#11) for a concrete reason: the call explicitly asks for AI-based approaches, a hierarchy of models, and seamless prediction from short-term to sub-seasonal scales to improve early warning for extreme events. That is almost word-for-word what #11 does — marine heatwave prediction using ML and data assimilation, with subseasonal forecasting and sea surface temperature as core concepts. The call also encourages integration with Copernicus and Destination Earth, which gives a natural operationalisation angle for an early-warning system.

The biggest doubt: the call is broad (any extreme event, continental to local scale), so a proposal would need to be framed tightly around marine heatwaves to stand out, and it expects a consortium with multiple lines of evidence (high-res Earth system models, retrospective analyses, case studies). That's a bigger ask than the project's current three-person team.

The other open grants on the project's slate are weaker fits:
- **#5** (Global Ocean Observing System, €50M, deadline 16 Feb 2027) is about observation infrastructure and governance, not prediction.
- **#2** (Antarctica/Southern Ocean, deadline 23 Sep 2027) is regionally specific and cryosphere-focused.
- **#7** (Disaster decision support, deadline 4 Nov 2027) is about civil-protection systems, not climate science.
- **#19** (NSF OTIC) is instrumentation development.
- **#20** (Carbon sources/sinks) and **#21** (Biodiversity data integration) are different scientific questions.

---

## 2. Who in the lab should lead

The nightly ranking and the requirement-slot analysis point to two people:

- **Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#18)** — declared interests in circulation and turbulence and physics-informed ML. He covers the "Earth system models" slot (declared: regional ocean models). His work on fast, physics-informed surrogates for ocean models maps directly onto the call's ask for improved prediction and projection modelling. He is a member of #11.

- **You, Mara (#14)** — declared interests in data assimilation with ML and ocean extremes. The ranking notes that the lab's specific focus on forecasting marine heatwaves using ML and data assimilation directly addresses the call's problem. You are the PI and a member of #11.

**Gaps no one in the lab covers:** extreme events in a changing climate (as a formal research area), digital twins, Copernicus integration, and Destination Earth. These would need to be filled by partners.

My read: **Tomás should lead the scientific core** (model hierarchy, physics-informed surrogates, prediction skill) and **you should lead the overall proposal** as PI, framing the marine heatwave early-warning application and the data-assimilation pipeline. That splits the two strongest declared strengths and keeps the project's own members at the centre.

---

## 3. Who outside the lab could partner

Collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so I can only tell you what the call itself suggests and what the gaps imply:

- **Copernicus Marine Service / ECMWF** — the call explicitly encourages integration with Copernicus and Destination Earth. A partner who can speak to operational SST forecasting and the Copernicus Marine Service would fill the "Copernicus" gap and give the proposal an operational-uptake story.
- **A high-resolution Earth system modelling group** — the call expects a "hierarchy of models" including high-res ESMs. No one in the lab declares ESM work, so a partner with that capability (e.g. a national meteorological service or a university climate-modelling group) would fill that gap.
- **A digital-twin or AI-for-climate group** — the call names digital twins specifically. No one in the lab declares this.
- **A low- to middle-income country partner** — the call encourages international cooperation with LMICs for capacity building, which is a plus for the proposal's score.

I could not run a co-authorship search to name specific people, so these are role descriptions rather than names. If you turn on collaborator search, I can look for specific researchers who match those gaps.

---

**One caveat:** I could not read the full project record for #11 (the call was denied), so I worked from the project's declared concepts, its members, and the grant text. If the project has a more detailed problem statement or milestones that I'm not seeing, the fit assessment could shift.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding, modelling, and predicting extreme events (isolated, compound, or cascading) in a changing climate, including their interaction, likelihood, and impact on resilience.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Utilizing a hierarchy of models (including high-resolution Earth system models and digital twins), data from past and recent climate, AI-based approaches, quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, and case studies to improve prediction, projection, and attribution capabilities across s…
