#12 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#5 [paper] A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period.
Authors: Zhenhua Zhang, Peng Chen, Siqi Zhang, Delu Pan
Venue: Science Advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aej4633
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The authors used 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP). A bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions, and low-light estimates were generated as physically const…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Arctic region, specifically marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions, using spaceborne LiDAR data from 2006 to 2023.
Abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year −1 during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Projects are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes:

- Effective and innovative methods for gathering, sharing and using large data sets in energy applications for the purpose of training AI models while ensuring privacy and security.

- Advanced and - wherever possible - open-source AI foundation models to support the digitalisation of the energy system, through improved grid observability, forecasting of supply and demand, advanced storage and renewables integration, demand side flexibility and energy efficiency.

- Enhanced cooperation, knowledge sharing and interoperability among energy system actors for secure and seamless data exchange.

- Advanced methodologies for AI model development ensuring that the results are FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) beyond the project ending, open source and accommodating for technology evolution.

Scope:

The quality of AI models depends strongly on the amount, quality, and representativeness of the data used for their training. Projects are expected to focus on developing, training and testing AI foundation models, using extensive data sets to accelerate the energy transition in key focus areas of the energy sector. Projects are expected to:

- Building on the results of previously funded projects on the Common European energy data space[1] as well as the ongoing work within the Data 4 Energy expert group, projects are expected to demonstrate innovative methods and data governance strategies for sharing data among various energy actors. Projects are expected to demonstrate that they have access to large relevant datasets at the time of submitting the proposal.

- Projects are expected to develop innovative strategies for sharing data in an effective, secure and transparent way to support the development of AI foundation models. An indicative non exhaustive list of strategies that can be explored is the use of data space connectors or federated training of models to allow the integration of confidential data; the creation of synthetic data as an intermediate step to fill data gaps or improve the quality of the data could also be explored. Projects could also explore other innovative data sharing strategies, such as an ‘AI gym’. The data governance strategies that will be developed in the project should be designed in a way to be scalable and operational even after the end of the project.

- Projects are expected to develop foundation models tailored for the energy sector, addressing at least one -or more- of the following use cases: planning and operation of electricity grids (including static power flow modelling and dynamic EMT modelling), forecasting, congestion management, anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, flexibility management, demand-side energy efficiency, smart and bidirectional charging of EVs or other use cases that contribute to the objective of digitalisation of the energy system.

- Projects are expected to perform in-depth testing and validation of developed foundation models in lab demonstrators and real-life pilots, building on the results and using the facilities of previously funded projects on “AI testing and experimentation facilities (TEFs)”[2]. Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic Ocean turbulent mixing is poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding, despite its importance for regional dynamics and global overturning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Training gradient-boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data to predict turbulent dissipation from hydrographic variables, using spatial block cross-validation for evaluation.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles) for training; pan-Arctic hydrographic observations and high-resolution model output for application.
Abstract:
Abstract Turbulent mixing may become increasingly important in a changing Arctic Ocean, influencing regional dynamics and global overturning. Arctic turbulence remains poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding. We train gradient‐boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles; ∼ data points) to predict turbulent dissipation from more widely available hydrography. Global training is essential for skill across non‐Arctic and Arctic regions (, 75% within a factor of 2 of observations; = 0.47–0.55 under spatial block cross‐validation). Applied to pan‐Arctic hydrographic observations, predictions show enhanced dissipation along margins and shelves and weaker values in basin interiors, consistent with current understanding. Applied to high‐resolution model output, predictions reveal diffusivities and a basin‐integrated irreversible buoyancy flux consistent with observations, yet markedly different from the common K‐Profile Parameterization—with implications for simulated tracer transport. Our parameterization can help assess climate‐mixing feedbacks in projections while physics‐based parameterizations mature.

Method (Mycelium's reading): Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model using a coupler named YAHO that links a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon, and energy components constrained by observations; the model uses an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave oc…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Simulations of approximately 1,000 years on one graphics processing unit; evaluation against observed climate data from 1979-2022; routing of runoff to 212 river gauges; and future projections for SSP1 and SSP3 scenarios for the period 2081-2100.
Abstract:
Earth system models underpin climate projections, but their cost limits how many scenarios, ensemble members and impact pathways can be explored. Machine-learning weather models forecast as skillfully as physics-based models at a fraction of the cost, yet coupled to an ocean they have produced weak El Nino variability or have learned it from climate-model output, and none carries the climate through rivers to the people exposed to it. Here we present Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model whose coupler, YAHO, yokes a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon and energy components constrained by observations. Adding the couplings one at a time shows what each contributes: over a climatological ocean the AI atmosphere varies from year to year by a third of the observed amount over the oceans, and an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave ocean, the residual of the observed sea surface temperature (SST) equation as stochastic forcing and the land's moisture flux raise this step by step and bring El Nino and its teleconnections, leaving the mean climate almost unchanged. The full model simulates about 1,000 years per day on one graphics processing unit, holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces the observed 1979-2022 global warming, carries forced change with a physically based structure around the frozen network (transient climate response 1.60 K), routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79 and, driven by emissions, separates the heatwave exposure of an SSP1 and an SSP3 world by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.

The one that matters most is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

Why it stands out for this project:

- **It is the proof-of-concept your project is trying to build.** The paper documents Australia's first pre-emptive rescue of a protected marine species: forecasts ahead of the 2023/24 El Niño flagged a high risk of marine heatwaves, an expert workshop judged the forecasted extremes (>20°C or +~3°C) a severe threat, and that triggered a real intervention — 25 red handfish captured in January 2024, held for three months, and released after the heatwave subsided, with post-release survival confirmed (#4, Abstract).
- **It closes the loop your project is missing.** Your project's whole point is that a forecast is only useful if it changes a decision. #4 shows the full chain — forecast → expert assessment → approved action → verified outcome — in a published, citable form. That is the template for what "early warning" is actually for.
- **It is recent and current.** It is in the feed as new this week (entered 2026-11-10) and is still open/current (#4).

The runner-up is **#5 — the 1–14-day machine-learning MHW forecast evaluation for the Northern Bay of Bengal** (Mojumder, 2026, Zenodo). It is the closest methodological match to your ML-forecasting side, and it is a data/code release, so it is directly reusable. But it is a thesis dataset with a thin abstract, and it evaluates skill against persistence benchmarks rather than showing what a forecast is *used for* — which is exactly what #4 demonstrates.

One caveat: I could not see the project's confirmed state (goals, blockers, milestones) in this conversation, so this ranking is based on the feed's own order and the papers' content. If the team has an open blocker on, say, the decision-trigger side of the system, #4 becomes even more central; if the blocker is purely forecast skill, #5 moves up. Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for a high-resolution, four-dimensional temperature climatology for Northern Chilean Patagonia to provide reference conditions for detecting anomalies, assessing ecosystem functioning, and identifying long-term trends in a region with complex fjords and channels where satellite observation…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Reconstruction of temperature fields using the Data Interpolating Variational Analysis (DIVAnd) tool from approximately three million in situ observations collected over 75 years, producing monthly fields from the surface to 400 m depth with a horizontal resolution of about 900 m and over 32 vertic…

Abstract:
Abstract. Ocean climatologies are essential for understanding the mean state and variability of marine systems, providing reference conditions for detecting anomalies, assessing ecosystem functioning and identifying long-term trends. In this study, we present the first high-resolution, four-dimensional temperature climatology for Northern Chilean Patagonia, a region characterised by the presence of a complex network of fjords and channels. The climatology was generated from approximately three million in situ observations collected over the past 75 years from multiple datasets. Using the Data Interpolating Variational Analysis (DIVAnd) tool, temperature fields were reconstructed with a horizontal resolution of about 900 m and over 32 vertical levels, producing monthly fields from the surface to 400 m depth. The resulting climatology accurately reproduces the main spatial and seasonal temperature patterns reported in previous studies. Surface temperatures show strong summer gradients between the open Pacific and Northern Patagonia, while enclosed regions such as Reloncaví Sound, Comau and Puyuhuapi Fjords exhibit pronounced seasonal amplitude compared with the more stable Corcovado Gulf. Below surface, temperature gradients become smoother and the thermocline deepens in summer, typically ranging between 10 and 50 m. At 100 m depth, temperatures are relatively constant throughout the year, but spatial variations are still observed, with Ancud Gulf and Reloncaví Sound being slightly warmer. This climatology provides a refined and physically consistent representation of the oceanographic structure of Northern Patagonia, offering an essential baseline for future modelling, monitoring and climate-change assessments in a region where satellite observations are limited by persistent cloud cover and complex topography. All climatologies generated in this study are freely available online.

final_text:
The one that matters most for Plastic pathways is **#7** — *Code and aggregated results for "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"* (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it stands out over the rest of the slate:

- **It is the only item squarely on the project's core question — where plastic actually ends up.** The paper develops a *tide-resolving beaching kernel* for OceanParcels 3.1.4, i.e. a mechanism for deciding when and where a drifting particle washes ashore, validated against real field records from Uido, South Korea. That is exactly the "last mile" of a pathways study: most of the slate is about observing the ocean (#3, #4, #5, #12), forecasting it (#6), or is off-topic (#11).
- **It is directly reusable.** The deposit ships the kernel code, the experiment scripts, and the aggregated results behind every number in the manuscript — so Jonah, Priya or you could drop the beaching logic into your own particle-tracking setup rather than reinventing it. The raw trajectories (~32 GB) and ROMS flow fields (~37 GB) are available on request if you want to reproduce their setup.
- **It addresses a known weakness in marine-litter models.** Most particle-tracking work treats the coast as a simple absorbing boundary; a tide-resolving kernel is a concrete, published answer to how tides push litter back and forth before it finally strands — which is what makes a "pathways" claim credible.

The runner-up is **#6** (*Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System*), which could supply the flow fields your particles drift in, but it's an input to the work, not the work itself. final_text:
Here's the comparison.

**#1 — GOOS / OceanEye (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)**
This is about strengthening the *infrastructure* of global ocean observation: deploying equipment, running observing-system experiments, network optimization, and co-creating technology roadmaps with industry. The emphasis is on continuity, openness, and EU strategic autonomy in observation capacity, with a strong biodiversity angle. It's a big, systems-level call.

**#2 — Antarctica & Southern Ocean (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)**
This is about *understanding and projecting* the future of the Southern Ocean and Antarctic cryosphere: ocean–atmosphere–sea-ice–ice interactions, tipping points, extreme events, ecosystem vulnerability, and improving Earth System Models and regional coupled models. It's a regional, process-and-projection call.

**Which fits Marine heatwave early warning better?**

Neither is a perfect match, but **#2 is the closer fit** for the project as it stands. Here's why:

- Your project's slate is dominated by *forecasting and prediction* work — ML-based MHW forecasts (#8), rapid-response strategies triggered by forecasts (#7), and ocean forecast system analyses (#13). #2 explicitly asks for improved projections, extreme events, and better Earth System / regional coupled models, which is the same intellectual territory.
- #1 is fundamentally about *observation infrastructure and governance* — deploying sensors, optimizing networks, procurement readiness. That's a different kind of project. Your lab's declared interests (data assimilation with ML, MHW prediction) sit closer to the modelling/prediction side than the infrastructure side.

**Caveats:**
- #2 is regionally scoped to Antarctica and the Southern Ocean. If your MHW early warning work is focused on other regions (e.g., the Bay of Bengal, as in #8), the geographic fit is weaker. You'd need to frame the project around Southern Ocean MHWs or argue that your methods transfer.
- #1 is much larger (€50M vs €5–11M) and has a much tighter deadline (Feb 2027 vs Sep 2027). If you were thinking of a bigger, multi-partner infrastructure-plus-prediction proposal, #1 could work, but it would require a different framing than what's currently on the project's slate.

**Bottom line:** If you're applying as the project is currently shaped — ML-driven MHW forecasting and early warning — **#2 is the better fit**, provided you can anchor it to the Southern Ocean region. #1 would require reframing the project around observation infrastructure, which is a bigger pivot.

Now I have a clear picture. Let me put this together.

---

## Best-fit grant: #2 — *Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate*

**Why it fits:** This is a Horizon Europe call (€3M–€15M, deadline **4 March 2027**) that explicitly asks for AI-based approaches, a hierarchy of models, and seamless prediction from short-term to multi-decadal scales to improve early warning for extreme events. Your project #11 — marine heatwave early warning, combining ocean data assimilation with ML — sits squarely in that space. The call names marine heatwaves as a type of extreme event, welcomes hybrid physics/data-driven forecasting, and encourages integration with Copernicus. The strongest single reason: the call's core ask (improve prediction and attribution of climate extremes with AI, feed early-warning systems) is almost word-for-word what your project does. The biggest doubt: the call is broad and competitive, and it expects a multi-model hierarchy and quantitative intercomparisons that go beyond a single lab's scope, so you'll need a strong consortium.

The other open grants I checked are weaker fits:
- **#10** (Global Ocean Observing System, €50M, deadline 16 Feb 2027) is about *observing infrastructure* and GOOS governance, not prediction.
- **#7** (AI for climate resilience at regional/local levels, deadline 21 Sep 2027) is about AI tools for *regional authorities and sectoral adaptation*, not ocean forecasting per se.
- **#5** (Disaster decision-support systems, deadline 4 Nov 2027) is about civil protection and crisis management, a different framing.
- **#1** (Digital energy systems) is off-topic.

---

## Who in the lab should lead

The nightly ranking and the requirement-slot analysis point to two people:

- **Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#18)** — the ranking names him first. His declared interest is *physics-informed ML*, and the analysis shows he covers the "Earth system models" slot (declared: regional ocean models). His work on fast, physics-informed surrogates for ocean models maps directly onto the call's ask for seamless prediction and projection modelling. He is also a member of project #11.

- **You, Mara (#14)** — the ranking names you second, on the strength of the lab's specific focus on marine heatwave forecasting with ML and data assimilation. As PI and project lead, you carry the overall vision and the data-assimilation expertise that the call's "hierarchy of models" language calls for.

**Practical suggestion:** You lead the application as PI (you own the project and the lab), with Tomás as the technical lead on the modelling/forecasting work package. Sun-hee Park (#17) is also on project #11 and could contribute on the data-tools and operationalisation side, though her declared interest (ocean data tools) is less central to this particular call.

**Gaps no one in the lab covers:** the call also asks for *digital twins*, *Copernicus integration*, and *Destination Earth* coordination. None of the five lab members declares these. You'll need to fill those slots with partners.

---

## Who outside the lab could partner

# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

#2 [grant] Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate
Amount: €3,000,000–€15,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL5-2027-01-D1-07
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-03-04
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding, modelling, and predicting extreme events (isolated, compound, or cascading) in a changing climate, including their interaction, likelihood, and impact on resilience.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Utilizing a hierarchy of models (including high-resolution Earth system models and digital twins), data from past and recent climate, AI-based approaches, quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, and case studies to improve prediction, projection, and attribution capabilities across s…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe and globally, encompassing large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena, with specific focus on EU and national/regional actors, low- to middle-income countries, and integration with initiatives like Copernicus and Destination Earth.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Improved understanding of past and present extreme events in the context of climate change in Europe and globally, as well as the interaction between different hazards, their cumulative and/or cascading effects.

- Enhanced seamless prediction and projection modelling and attribution capabilities for extreme events and their likelihood to support preparedness, response and resilience to climate change by EU and national and regional actors. The EU Union Preparedness Strategy, the EU Adaptation Strategy and the European Climate Adaptation Plan can act as a guidance in these efforts.

- Up-to-date contributions towards latest climate science, risk assessments, adaptation strategies and policies and improved early warning systems for single and multi-hazard events.

Scope:

Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of extreme events. Understanding and predicting extreme events and the interaction between different types of hazards is critical for building resilience and safeguarding communities.

Actions are expected to draw upon multiple lines of evidence from a hierarchy of models (including high resolution Earth system models and digital twins) and data of past and recent climate to further our understanding of processes, pre-conditioning and causality driving extreme events under climate change conditions, including anthropogenic factors and internal variability. Other innovative and efficient modelling and analysis methods, including AI-based approaches, to better predict, emulate and reveal climate change related extreme and unprecedented high impact events, and to capture their likelihood are particularly welcome.

Extreme events should be addressed in their broadest sense and types, encompassing isolated, compound or cascading events affecting lives, livelihoods, ecosystems, socio-economic sectors and infrastructures, from large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena.

Actions should encompass quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, lessons learned and case studies of recent emblematic and diverse extreme events, and demonstrate the corresponding progress offered by the project in terms of improved understanding, comprehensive integration of multiple lines of evidence, and seamless (e.g. from short-term weather to sub-seasonal and multi-decadal scales) prediction and projection capabilities and skills.

The work is expected to support the future European Climate Risk Assessment (EUCRA)[1], for example through storylines on extremes or other approaches. Project outcomes should demonstrate clear benefits for the prediction and attribution of extreme events and contribute to the activities of the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change.

Cooperation with global, EU, national and regional actors in the field of Disaster Risk Reduction and climate adaptation, including through integration into or interoperability with Copernicus, Destination Earth and other relevant initiatives is encouraged. In addition, international cooperation with low- to middle-income countries automatically eligible for Horizon Europe funding[2] is encouraged in support of climate resilience efforts, especially for capacity building.

Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice and technical support in the context of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service and transfer of relevant research outcomes to operations.

This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the new Extreme-Events Flagship Cluster. Successful consortia will be asked to coordinate with projects to be selected under ESA's FutureEO programme to facilitate access to and uptake of satellite data products and related tools or methodologies. Method (Mycelium's reading): Development and testing of AI-powered tools (including deep learning and machine learning) to process big datasets, improve data integrity/accessibility, and optimize resource management in specific sectors. Proposals must demonstrate advancement beyond the state of the art, engage private sector a…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European regions and local authorities. Objective 1 requires testing with at least 3 regional and local authorities. Objective 2 requires testing in the territory of at least 5 regional or local authorities, engaging private sector actors in sectors such as smart agriculture, construction, water ma…
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

AI has the potential to support or facilitate virtually every aspect of regions’ climate adaptation efforts. From risk assessment to climate forecasting, from infrastructure planning to resource management, and more. Contributing to the objectives of the AI Continent Action Plan and the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change, projects are expected to contribute one of the following:

- AI is used to improve actionable climate adaptation knowledge for European regions and local authorities by integrating climate data into decision-making processes.

- Specific sectors in the selected regions become more resilient to climate change thanks to the use of AI to improve their processes or technologies, while simultaneously advancing their digital transformation.

Scope:

Rationale

Over the past few years, a rapid and disruptive acceleration of progress in Artificial Intelligence has occurred, driven by significant advances in widespread data availability, computing power and machine learning[1]. While the potential of Artificial Intelligence is being uncovered each day and its possibilities are expanding exponentially, such technological revolution can significantly accelerate Europe’s efforts towards climate resilience and contribute to the objectives of the Adaptation Mission.

Considering the ever-changing nature of AI growth, proposals should demonstrate that they go beyond state of the art, they should identify a specific gap that can be addressed by an AI-powered tool, and explain why it would improve existing models, tools or applications or, alternatively, justify the need to develop entirely new solutions.

In particular, the proposal should address one of the following two objectives:

Objective 1: “AI for more accessible data”

AI can quickly process and identify patterns from big datasets that would otherwise be too complex. Proposals should explore how AI can be further integrated, including via AI techniques such as deep learning, to make data more accessible and understandable, to facilitate informed decision-making by regions and local authorities. Improvements should be tested with at least 3 regional and local authorities to ensure that they provide a concrete added value to end-users (i.e. decision-makers). Moreover, proposals are expected to apply such analysis to concretely improve data integrity and accessibility[2].

Objective 2: “AI for sectoral adaptation”

Use and application of machine learning and AI tools to help regions and local authorities optimize their management of resources and improve adaptation technologies in key sector(s). Proposals should develop and test the tools in the territory of at least 5 regional or local authorities. The work should engage private sector actors with relevant expertise in the sector chosen (e.g. smart agriculture, construction and buildings sector, water management, waste management, transports, resilience of energy systems, etc.), to ensure that such AI-powered tools are designed for scalability and uptake.

Regardless of the objective addressed, all proposals should provide training and dissemination material for different target groups, including regions and local authorities, on how to best take advantage of the AI-powered improvements. Attention should be given to avoiding biases and ensuring that the data is representative of diverse populations, as well as taking into account possible limitations and potential misinformation when using generative AI tools.

To ensure a balanced portfolio covering both objectives, grants will be awarded to proposals not only in order of ranking but at least also to one proposal that is the highest ranked within each objective, provided that the applications attain all thresholds. To this purpose, the objective addressed by each proposal should also be specified in the free keywords section of the proposal (e.g. ‘objective 1’ or ‘objective 2’).

#24 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

#20 [paper] Ensemble Covariance Propagation with Machine Learning Weather Prediction Models in a Realistic Data Assimilation System
Authors: Simon S. Toedtli, D. Ahijevych, Wei Wang, C. Snyder
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/03f85b56ec35cf96a456064e52b1e9890ec3b1dd
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Integrating machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models into classical data assimilation (DA) workflows requires that they accurately evolve ensemble covariances.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A two-way coupled DA system where an ensemble variational (EnVar) component evolves the mean and an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) evolves the covariances. The system uses the MLWP model GraphCast for the EnKF and the physics-based MPAS model for the EnVar, cycled over one month.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A realistic DA cycling system assimilating a wide range of real-world observations, including microwave radiances, over a one-month period.
Abstract:
Integrating machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models into classical data assimilation (DA) workflows requires that they accurately evolve ensemble covariances. We evaluate this capability in a two-way coupled DA system, where an ensemble variational (EnVar) component evolves the mean and an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) evolves the covariances. The system is cycled over one month and assimilates a wide range of real-world observations, including microwave radiances. Using the MLWP model GraphCast for the EnKF and the physics-based MPAS model for the EnVar yields ensemble spread and covariances comparable to a reference configuration in which MPAS evolves both components. The resulting EnVar mean achieves consistently lower RMSE against GFS analyses, except near the model top, where spurious correlations degrade performance. These results demonstrate that MLWP models can propagate covariance information in a realistic DA cycling system and provide a proof of concept for their integration into future operational ensemble systems.

These systems should leverage cutting-edge AI-driven tools to process large volumes of data, providing actionable insights that improve decision-making during critical moments, such as from early warning to early action. Emphasis should be placed on integrating advanced data analysis and predictive modelling to anticipate disaster developments and guide interventions, while ensuring that the systems are transparent, explainable, and built on principles of trustworthiness, inclusive and gender sensitive and ethical AI use and on secure AI deployments.

Projects should conduct a stakeholder or market analysis and a roadmap or plan for uptake of the developed methodologies, findings, and technologies to the industry, the research and innovation community, and/or the relevant authorities.

Additionally, test centres should play a key role in this research by increasing their capacity to trial and validate emerging technologies, supporting more effective civil preparedness and crisis response capabilities.

The expected outcome is to create systems that not only enhance operational efficiency and response times but also foster better collaboration among stakeholders, including local authorities, emergency services, and other relevant actors. This includes integrating drones with state emergency vehicles, smart traffic systems, and law enforcement to enhance data driven disaster preparedness and emergency response, ensuring effective coordination and faster decision-making for local authorities.

Projects should also contribute to improving the usability and accessibility of decision-support systems for diverse users, ensuring they are easily integrated into disaster management frameworks and can be used effectively in different crisis situations. The solutions should align with EU guidelines on AI ethics[1] and resilience-building, ensuring they complement existing civil protection and crisis management initiatives while driving innovation in disaster risk reduction. The Preparedness Union Strategy is a key document in this regard. Analysing the capacity gaps of the UCPM[2] and finding synergies with projects from operational grants, such as the Knowledge for Action in Prevention & Preparedness (KAPP)[3], is recommended.

In this topic the integration of the gender dimension (sex and gender analysis) in research and innovation content should be addressed only if relevant in relation to the objectives of the research effort.

Method (Mycelium's reading): The project involves validating and scaling AI tools in demo sites and operational grids, demonstrating an AI development environment integrated with the digital spine and digital twin, and prototyping machine learning at edge nodes and federated systems using agent-based architectures, incremental…

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes:

- Advanced, secure frugal (energy-, resource-, data- and cost-efficient, sustainable) AI tools for real-time grid operations (including protection), market operations (if relevant) and consumer empowerment in distributed energy systems.

- A demonstrated AI development environment integrated with the upgraded digital spine of the energy system and energy-saving consumer applications.

final_text:
Here's what I found, with the honest caveats:

## Best fit: #13 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System

Of the ten open grants on the Plastic pathways slate, #13 is the strongest match. The project's core question — how plastic moves through the ocean and where it ends up — is fundamentally an *observation* problem: you need sustained, coordinated in-situ and satellite-based monitoring to track pathways, quantify fluxes, and attribute sources. #13 funds exactly that: stabilising and operationalising the global ocean observing system, with explicit hooks to climate resilience and biodiversity conservation. The lab's declared strengths in satellite oceanography (#30) and data assimilation (#28) map directly onto its "strengthen observing capacities and data coordination" slots.

The next-best candidates are weaker:
- **#14 Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination** — broad, but no lab member's declared profile covers its instrumentation slot; the nightly ranking only gives 62–65% "closest match" scores, which is thin.
- **#15 Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity** — Priya covers the satellite slot, but the call leans heavily on omics, Copernicus/Galileo services, and biodiversity frameworks that no one here declares.
- **#10 ZEWT (waterborne transport impact)** — relevant to plastic sources from shipping, but the call is about transport *infrastructure* impacts, not pathway modelling per se.

## Who should lead

**Jonah Whitcombe (#29)** is the natural lead. He's the only lab member who declares *marine litter* as an interest, and he's already a member of the Plastic pathways project. He's the person whose profile the reviewers will look for first.

**Priya Raman (#30)** should co-lead or take the observing-systems work package — she covers the satellite remote sensing slot that #13 explicitly asks for, and the nightly ranking named her top for that call.

**You (#28)** bring the data-assimilation and ML-for-forecasting angle, which strengthens the "operationalise the system" part of the proposal. The ranking placed you second for #13.

**Sun-hee (#31)** and **Tomás (#32)** are less central here; their declared interests (data tools, circulation/turbulence) are useful but not the core of this call.

## Who outside the lab

This is where I have to be straight with you: **I could not finish this part.** I checked co-authorship introduction paths to all four other lab members and found none that run only through people you can already see. I also don't have a function to search for external researchers or labs by topic — the collab search is turned off on this instance. So I can't name a specific external partner with evidence.

What I *can* say from the call text: #13 asks for industry partners and coverage of areas beyond national jurisdiction, neither of which anyone in the lab covers. You'd want at least one partner with a track record in ocean observing network operations (e.g., a national oceanographic institute or a GOOS node) and ideally one industry or technology partner. I'd suggest you look at the consortium requirements in the full call text and check who has applied to similar observing-system calls before — that's a search I can't run for you here.

**What I could not finish:** naming specific external partners with evidence. If collab search were available, or if you could tell me a researcher or lab you have in mind, I could check their profile and introduction path.

#24 [grant] Long-term drivers and consequences of soil degradation: learning from the past to improve future soil health
Amount: €5,500,000–€12,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-MISS-2027-05-SOIL-06-two-stage
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-04-08
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Activities under this topic will help progress towards the objectives and targets of the Mission Soil and the EU Soil Strategy for 2030. Moreover, activities should also contribute to meeting the ambitions of the Sustainable Development Goals[1].

Project results are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes:

- policymakers and other relevant stakeholders have improved access to knowledge and quantitative data on changes in soil degradation over the past centuries to millennia across different pedo-climatic regions, alongside projections for future soil health trends under different scenarios;

- policymakers, land managers and other relevant stakeholders have an advanced understanding of the long-term drivers (and the similarities and differences with short-term drivers) and long-term consequences of soil degradation processes including their role in the climate and biodiversity systems and in the water and nutrient cycles, both in the past and in the future;

- policymakers and other relevant stakeholders have an expanded comprehension of the social and cultural factors driving historical soil degradation and societal perceptions of soil degradation and soil health, as well as an enhanced understanding of the long-term socio-economic consequences of soil degradation processes, e.g. in terms of EU’s agricultural competitiveness, both in the past and in the future;

- citizens are more aware of the societal impacts of soil degradation and the lengthy recovery process, to foster an accelerated acceptance of sustainable soil management practices.

Scope:

Since the beginning of agriculture, human activities worldwide have contributed to soil degradation, including soil erosion, soil compaction and loss of soil organic carbon among others. This caused problems to farmers and landowners, as well as to society in general. However, our knowledge of changes in soil health over the past centuries to millennia is limited, and available datasets span only the past two or three decades. This knowledge gap hinders a thorough understanding of the long-term drivers and consequences of soil degradation, of improved future projections of soil health under different scenarios of climate and land management changes, of the long-term effects of soil management practices, as well as of how human behaviour can change to adopt measures to increase soil health. This is especially relevant in the context of future climate change.

Proposals should:

- study past soil degradation processes and their socio-economic, cultural and natural drivers and consequences across different pedo-climatic regions, based on multiple lines of evidence coming from, for instance, historical documents, historical records, archaeological data, sediment archives, buried fossil soils and archived soil and plant samples;

- apply, validate and advance the development of methodologies to study past soil health, using techniques such as ancient eDNA analysis, pollen, spores, environmental radionuclides and other proxy indicators, and implement a multi-scalar approach to integrate these data at the scale of pedo-climatic regions;

- utilise numerical models and digital tools to reconstruct past soil degradation patterns and predict future trends and develop trajectories for sustainable soil management;

- encourage citizen and stakeholder involvement through active participation in the data collection and data analysis with citizen science initiatives, as well as carry out communication and awareness raising activities on the long-term changes of soil health and the societal impact of soil degradation.

In carrying out the activities, consortia should work in an interdisciplinary way bringing disciplines, expertise and approaches from the soil sciences, environmental sciences and social sciences and humanities (including history, archaeology, sociology and social geography).

Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-CIRCBIO-05
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-22
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- all relevant stakeholders, including consumers, economic and social economy operators and waste managers, have an improved understanding of the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits to circularity in the footwear industry;

- economic operators and waste managers are provided with evidence-based, innovative, cost-effective, and scalable solutions that improve the management of end-of-life footwear products, valorise post-consumer footwear waste materials and increase the circularity of the value chain;

- consumers have access to user-friendly solutions to correctly dispose of end-of-life footwear, thus reducing landfill, improving sustainability practices, supporting them in making more conscious choices, and contributing to climate change mitigation and adaptation by reducing waste and promoting circular economy practices.

Scope:

The transition to a circular economy requires innovative solutions to manage end-of-life products, including footwear, which can have significant environmental and climate impacts if landfilled and not properly collected, sorted, and recycled. In line with the EU's ambitious circular economy targets and policies, such as the Waste Framework Directive and the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, this topic aims at improving the circularity of the footwear value chain and reducing the environmental footprint of end-of-life post-consumer footwear, whilst promoting a more regenerative and restorative approach to the footwear value chain.

Proposals should:

- assess the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits linked to the transition of the footwear industry towards circularity, particularly in the collection, sorting and recycling of post-consumer footwear waste;

- develop and test new methods and technologies that facilitate the collection, sorting, preparation for reuse and recycling of post-consumer footwear products, integrating digital tools (including AI) and the use of the Digital Product Passport to enable reuse and recycling, and minimise the release of hazardous chemicals and microplastics during the recycling process;

- explore and develop innovative business models that enable the transition towards a circular and sustainable footwear value chain, promote the uptake of design for preparing for reuse and recycling, enable the development of take-back solutions and stimulate informed consumer choices and sustainable consumption patterns;

- develop and test innovative solutions that facilitate the collaboration between the relevant stakeholders, including footwear manufacturers, retailers, consumers and waste managers, to ensure the effectiveness and uptake of the proposed solutions, including strategies for managing hazardous chemicals and microplastics in footwear waste.

Successful proposals should bring together all relevant stakeholders active in the footwear value chain, namely industry representatives, SMEs, brand owners, producers, retailers, local authorities, waste managers, economic operators, consumer organisations, researchers, and NGOs.

The topic supports EU policies, particularly the European Green Deal, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and its working plan, as well as the zero pollution action plan. The proposed solutions should also be consistent with the Waste Framework Directive, the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for textiles, the Clean Industrial Deal and the EU Circular Economy Act, supporting Europe’s efforts to develop a single market for sustainable products.

This topic requires the effective contribution of SSH disciplines and the involvement of SSH experts, institutions as well as the inclusion of relevant SSH expertise, in order to produce meaningful and significant effects enhancing the societal impact of the related research activities.

#5 [grant] Textile circularity through advanced processing and manufacturing technologies and system approaches (IA) (Textiles for the Future partnership)
Amount: €200,000–€12,500,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL4-2027-01-MAT-PROD-08
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-02-02
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

- Increased economically viable and functionally equivalent renewable material and sustainable chemical solutions used in large scale textile applications, including apparel, home and technical textiles;

- A realistic pathway for an absolute reduction of the use of virgin fossil-based materials and chemicals used to produce textile products for the EU market by 2035, contributing to enhance the preservation of human health, biodiversity and ecosystems, whether aquatic or terrestrial ecosystem preservation and emission reduction;

- Uptake of business models and system approaches that allow for the scale up of sustainable textile material and chemical alternatives as competitive alternatives to conventional approaches.

Scope:

Innovative renewable textile fibres and sustainable chemical solutions today face almost insurmountable cost disadvantages compared to extremely cost-competitive and industrially entrenched fibres and chemicals based on virgin fossil resources. To allow for the scale up of the use of innovative renewable materials and sustainable chemicals by the textile industry, improved processability of materials, suitable processing technology, deeper technical knowledge and smart phase-in approaches such as material blending or drop-in solutions are required. Specific emphasis must be placed on resulting final product quality, their durability and functionality to avoid negative user/consumer perception of products made with renewable materials and sustainable chemicals. As not all cost and quality challenges may be immediately overcome by technological innovation, accompanying business models and systems approaches are needed to enable equitable cost and risk sharing among all involved stakeholders in the textile value chain.

Attributes such as recyclability, recycled material content, and resource efficiency as well as reduced carbon and environmental footprint are expected to be part of the textile-specific requirements under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation.

Proposals should specifically address:

- Innovative processing technologies to facilitate the efficient use of recycled, regenerated and bio-based fibres as well as sustainable processing and functionalising chemicals across all major stages of the textile manufacturing value chain, such as spinning, weaving, knitting, dyeing or finishing;

- Quantification of biodiversity outcomes associated to new processes by using existing Monitoring, Reporting and Validation (MRV) methodologies, adapting and testing them if needed;

- Characterisation, quality assurance and mitigation strategies for the most common processing and functionality challenges and limitations of the sustainable materials and chemicals targeted;

- Development of best practices and training materials targeted at designers, manufacturers, brands, end of life managers and end users, working with the targeted materials and chemicals;

- Strategies and tools to practically implement collective risk sharing and smart scaling approaches.

Proposals should actively involve suppliers of renewable materials and sustainable chemicals, brands, commercial end users and developers/manufacturers of relevant processing technology and industrial partners with the capacity to commercially scale up production with the targeted materials and chemicals. The involvement of partners beyond the manufacturing supply chain, such as product designers, brands, commercial end users and end of life managers including collectors, sorters, recyclers and remanufacturers is particularly encouraged. Proposals should carry out research and innovation to develop missing elements and achieve the necessary integration, including economic viability. Hence, synergies with, or using results from, other projects may be appropriate. The mere integration of existing technologies or processes is outside the scope of this topic.

Here's the corrected summary.

## Where the project stands

**Plastic pathways** (#2) is a lab-level project with three members: Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you. The project's confirmed state — goals, method, stage, milestones, open blockers — is not visible to me right now. If the team has filled in the project description in the app, I'd pick it up; if not, that's the first thing worth doing, since it's what Mylo uses to rank the slate and tie new items to specific blockers.

## Three most relevant new papers

All three entered the slate this week (since 2026-11-10):

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The most direct match: a three-phase beaching kernel for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories. If Plastic pathways involves particle tracking of litter to shore, this is the one to read first — the code and aggregated results are deposited, so it's also a ready-made methodological template.

2. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, Remote Sensing). Relevant on the methods side: a YOLO11-based detector (with Dynamic Snake Convolution and CBAM) for low-contrast, curved ocean features from MODIS imagery. The paper reports detection F1 of 86.00% and segmentation F1 of 87.55%, the highest among the methods evaluated. If the project uses satellite imagery to track plastic or debris, this is a strong candidate for adapting the detection pipeline.

3. **#11 — "Basin-scale changes in net primary production from the biogeochemical-Argo array"** (Ryan-Keogh & Thomalla, 2026, Science Advances). Relevant for the observing-systems context: it demonstrates how autonomous profiling floats fill gaps that satellite-only observation can't, and explicitly calls for integrated observing systems. Useful if Plastic pathways needs to justify in-situ sampling infrastructure alongside remote sensing.

The other new items (#4 LiDAR Arctic NPP, #5 PROMOM daily analyses, #7 Northeast Pacific seasonal forecast, #9 multi-agent tracking) are further afield from plastic pathways.

## One funding opportunity

**#3 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation"** (Horizon Europe, €50M, deadline 2027-02-16). This is the strongest fit on the slate: it funds deployment of ocean observation equipment, observing system experiments, and network optimization, with explicit attention to biodiversity and ecosystem knowledge. A plastic pathways project that combines in-situ sampling (e.g., float-based or coastal sensor networks) with satellite observation and particle-tracking modelling maps well onto its call for "interconnected physical, biogeochemical and biological components relevant to biodiversity conservation." The deadline gives you about three months to shape a proposal.

A second option, if the project leans more toward data infrastructure than hardware: **#12 — "Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity"** (Horizon, €3–8M, deadline 2027-09-22), which is more about FAIR data integration and AI analytics across sensors.

If you'd like, I can pull the full text of #6 or #10 to dig into the methods in more detail.

Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-BIODIV-01
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-22
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

- develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. Proposals should take into account socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems, including land and sea use and emissions of pollutants (e.g. agriculture, aquaculture, urbanization, resource exploitation and management practices). Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor
