Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The authors used 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP). A bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions, and low-light estimates were generated as physically const…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Arctic region, specifically marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions, using spaceborne LiDAR data from 2006 to 2023.
Abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year −1 during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#11 [paper] Basin-scale changes in net primary production from the biogeochemical-Argo array.
Authors: Thomas James Ryan-Keogh, Sandy Thomalla
Venue: Science Advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeb0994
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Estimating basin-scale changes in marine net primary production (NPP) while overcoming the limitation of remote sensing, which is restricted to surface observations and cannot capture subsurface variability.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Using data from the biogeochemical-Argo array of autonomous profiling floats to estimate basin-scale NPP change via the carbon-based production algorithm.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The biogeochemical-Argo array, covering the Atlantic, Southern, and Pacific Oceans.
Abstract:
Marine net primary production is expected to be affected by climate change. Although remote sensing offers broad spatial and temporal coverage, it is limited to surface observations and cannot capture subsurface variability. Autonomous profiling floats provide critical depth-resolved measurements that help bridge this gap. Here, we use data from the biogeochemical-Argo array to estimate basin-scale change in net primary production using the carbon-based production algorithm. We find statistically significant negative trends across the Atlantic and Southern Oceans and positive trends in the Pacific Ocean. These changes, if occurring in response to climate forcing, raise concern due to the key role of phytoplankton productivity in sustaining marine ecosystems. These trends typically agree in direction and magnitude with those from satellites. Our findings highlight the value of the biogeochemical-Argo array in detecting change in ocean productivity, demonstrating its potential for sustained monitoring. These results underscore the need for integrated observing systems to capture the full extent of changing marine productivity.

Here's what I found. Across both projects, the two most urgent deadlines are:

**1. #14 — 10th International Conference on Geoinformatics and Data Analysis**
- Deadline: 2026-11-20 (manuscript), 7 days away
- Project: Marine heatwave early warning (#1)
- Best fit in lab: **Mara Ellison** (declared interests: data assimilation with ML, ocean extremes) or **Tomás Ferreira-Lind** (circulation and turbulence, physics-informed ML)
- Paper to strengthen the application: **#39** — "Evaluation of 1-14-Day Machine-Learning Forecasts of Marine Heatwaves in the Northern Bay of Bengal Against Persistence Benchmarks" (Mojumder, 2026). This is a direct methodological match: ML-based MHW forecasting evaluated against persistence benchmarks, which is exactly the kind of evidence a geoinformatics/data-analysis conference would want to see.

**2. #29 — 47th IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS)**
- Deadline: 2027-01-11 (abstract + manuscript), ~2 months away
- Project: Plastic pathways (#2)
- Best fit in lab: **Priya Raman** (declared interests: satellite oceanography, coastal water quality) or **Jonah Whitcombe** (marine litter, Lagrangian analysis)
- Paper to strengthen the application: **#38** — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea" (Rong et al., 2026). This demonstrates the lab's capacity for satellite-based ocean feature detection, which pairs well with a plastic-pathways submission that relies on remote sensing to track debris.

---

**Caveat:** #29's deadline is in January, so it's the next most urgent *after* #14. If you want the two *closest* deadlines regardless of project, #14 (Nov 20) and #11 (Sandia von Neumann Fellowship, Nov 18) are the two nearest — but #11 is a postdoc fellowship, not a project application. Let me know if you'd like me to dig into #11 or any other item.

#37 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#38 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Here's the comparison, grounded in what each call actually asks for and what the Marine heatwave early warning project (#3) is about.

## The two grants at a glance

| | #1 GOOS / OceanEye | #2 Antarctica & Southern Ocean |
|---|---|---|
| **Focus** | Strengthening the *global observing system* — deploying equipment, observing-system experiments, network optimization, tech roadmaps with industry | *Understanding and projecting* the Antarctic/Southern Ocean — ocean–ice–atmosphere interactions, decadal-to-millennial projections, tipping points, ecosystem vulnerability |
| **Core question** | How do we keep global ocean observations continuous, open and resilient (esp. in under-observed regions)? | How do we reduce uncertainty in the future state of the Southern Ocean and its impacts? |
| **Amount** | €50,000,000 | €5,000,000–€11,000,000 |
| **Deadline** | 2027-02-16 | 2027-09-23 |

## Which fits the Marine heatwave early warning project better?

**#1 (GOOS / OceanEye) is the stronger fit**, for three reasons:

1. **It's about the data backbone your project runs on.** Marine heatwave early warning is fundamentally a *forecasting* problem — it needs reliable, continuous, well-placed observations (SST, in-situ and satellite) to feed and validate models. #1 is explicitly about closing structural gaps in the observing network, running observing-system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), and network optimization — exactly the kind of work that makes a heatwave early-warning system more skillful and trustworthy.

2. **The scope overlaps directly.** #1 calls out "under-observed regions" and the need for "reliable services" and "data delivery that is fit-for-purpose." A heatwave early-warning service is precisely a fit-for-purpose service built on that data. #2, by contrast, is anchored to the Antarctic continental shelves, bottom-water formation, sea-ice/ice-sheet dynamics and long-term (decadal-to-millennial) projections — a different region and a different timescale than operational heatwave forecasting.

3. **Timescale and purpose align.** #1 is about *operationalizing* observations for near-term, decision-relevant services. #2 is about *understanding and projecting* a specific polar region over decades to centuries. An early-warning project lives in the operational, near-term world, which is #1's home.

## One honest caveat

I couldn't open the full project record — #3 only returned its name and members (Mara, Tomás Ferreira-Lind, Sun-hee Park), not its confirmed problem statement, method or stage. So this fit is judged from the project's *purpose* (marine heatwave early warning) and your declared interests (ocean data assimilation with ML, marine heatwave prediction, SST forecasting), not from a detailed read of the project's current state. If the project has a specific regional focus or a particular methodological angle you'd like me to weigh in, tell me and I'll sharpen the comparison.

**Bottom line:** go after **#1 (GOOS / OceanEye)** — it's the observing-system call that underpins a heatwave early-warning service, and its €50M scale and Feb 2027 deadline make it the more substantial and more relevant target. #2 is a solid polar-science call but aimed at a different region and timescale.

# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is

2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,

3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

Here's what I found.

## Which open grant fits best

Two open grants are on the project's slate: #3 (EU, €50M, deadline 2027-02-16) and #10 (NSF OTIC, deadline 2027-02-15).

**#10 Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (NSF) is the better fit.** It funds unsolicited proposals for instrumentation development that enhances observational, experimental, or analytical capabilities for the ocean science community. That lines up with Plastic pathways' core method: the project's slate includes a tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter particle tracking (#7), which is exactly the kind of reusable analytical tool OTIC is built for.

#3 (the EU GOOS call) is a much bigger, infrastructure-scale call about strengthening the global observing system, governance frameworks and EU strategic autonomy. It's not a bad thematic home for ocean observation work, but it's aimed at large consortia and global-scale observing networks rather than a single lab's tool development — a much heavier lift for a 3-person project.

Biggest doubt on #10: I can't see the full eligibility rules (institution type, PI citizenship) in what's stored, so check the grants.gov page before committing.

The nightly ranking for #10 named:
- **Tomás Ferreira-Lind** (#18) — closest match to his research profile (65%)

Collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so I can't surface external candidates. One concrete lead from the project's own slate: **Sehan Lim and Sunwook Hong**, authors of the beaching kernel paper (#7) — they've built the particle-tracking tooling this project works with and would be natural partners for an OTIC proposal. I couldn't look up their affiliations (not visible to me), so you'd need to check their paper for contact details.

## Where the project stands

The project record I can see is thin. **Plastic pathways** (#2) is a lab project with three members — Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you — but no confirmed goals, stage, milestones, or blockers are recorded, and I can't see when its state was last confirmed, so it may be out of date. If you update the project's goals and status in the app, I can give a sharper review next time.

## Three most relevant new papers

All three entered the slate this week (since 2026-11-10):

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The most directly relevant: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields. If your project tracks where plastic goes and where it ends up, this is a ready-made method and codebase to build on or benchmark against.
2. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, *Remote Sensing*). A YOLO11-based framework (with Dynamic Snake Convolution and CBAM) for detecting and segmenting low-contrast, curved ocean features from MODIS imagery. The paper reports detection F1 of 86.00% and segmentation F1 of 87.55%, the highest among the methods it evaluated. The transferable lesson is a template for automating detection of hard-to-see surface features from satellite data — useful if part of your pathway work involves spotting debris or surface signatures from space.
3. **#5 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model"** (Zhang, 2026, Zenodo). A data release of daily analyses from a regional ocean forecast system. Potentially relevant as a forcing/flow-field source for particle-tracking of plastic transport, though I can only see the title and deposit record — no abstract is stored, so treat the details as unverified.

The other new items on the slate (#4, #7, #9, #11) concern phytoplankton, seasonal forecasting, multi-agent tracking, and biogeochemical Argo — none speak directly to plastic pathways.

## One funding opportunity

**#3 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation"** (Horizon Europe, HORIZON-NATURE-2027-04-01). €50M, deadline **16 February 2027**, still open. It funds strengthening the GOOS: deploying observation equipment, observing system experiments, network optimisation, and technology roadmaps with industry, with attention to structural gaps in under-observed regions. A plastic-pathways angle fits naturally — e.g. a coordinated observing and modelling effort to track debris transport and beaching in under-observed areas, combining in-situ records with model-based particle tracking, and co-creating a roadmap with coastal managers and industry. The size and infrastructure emphasis make it a strong fit for a lab-scale project that wants to scale up its observation capacity.

A second option worth keeping in your pocket: **#8 — NSF Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC)**, deadline 15 February 2027, which supports instrumentation development with broad applicability to ocean science — a good fit if you want to develop a new sensor or tracking method for debris.

**Suggested next steps:** confirm the project's goals and current stage in the app so I can tie the slate to specific blockers; and if #3 interests you, I can walk through a fit assessment in more detail.

The other new items on the slate (#4, #7, #9, #11) are about phytoplankton, seasonal forecasting, multi-agent tracking, and biogeochemical Argo — none of which speak directly to plastic pathways.

## One funding opportunity

**#3 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation"** (Horizon Europe, HORIZON-NATURE-2027-04-01). €50M, deadline **16 February 2027**, still open. It funds strengthening the GOOS: deploying observation equipment, observing system experiments, network optimisation, and technology roadmaps with industry, with attention to structural gaps in under-observed regions. A plastic-pathways angle fits naturally — e.g. a coordinated observing and modelling effort to track debris transport and beaching in under-observed areas, combining in-situ records with model-based particle tracking, and co-creating a roadmap with coastal managers and industry. The size and the infrastructure emphasis make it a strong fit for a lab-scale project that wants to scale up its observation capacity.

A second option worth keeping in your pocket: **#8 — NSF Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC)**, deadline 15 February 2027, which supports instrumentation development with broad applicability to ocean science — a good fit if you want to develop a new sensor or tracking method for debris.

**Suggested next steps:** confirm the project's goals and current stage in the app so I can tie the slate to specific blockers; and if #3 interests you, I can walk through a fit assessment for it in more detail.

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#7 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

final_text:
Here's the picture across both projects. The two most urgent deadlines in the next 60 days are:

## 1. #14 — 10th International Conference on Geoinformatics and Data Analysis
**Deadline: 2026-11-20 (in 7 days) — manuscript**
**Project: Marine heatwave early warning (#1)**

**Who fits:**
- **Priya Raman (#6)** — closest profile match (59%), declared interests in satellite oceanography and coastal water quality
- **Mara Ellison (#4)** — 58% match, data assimilation with ML and ocean extremes
- **Jonah Whitcombe (#5)** — 58% match, marine litter and Lagrangian analysis

**Paper to strengthen the application:**
- **#37** — "Evaluation of 1-14-Day Machine-Learning Forecasts of Marine Heatwaves in the Northern Bay of Bengal Against Persistence Benchmarks" (Mojumder, 2026). This is directly on-topic: ML-based MHW forecasting evaluated against persistence baselines. It would anchor a submission on the skill and validation of short-range MHW forecasts.
- **#36** — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish" (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026) could complement it by showing the real-world impact of a forecast-driven intervention.

## 2. #29 — 47th IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS)
**Deadline: 2027-01-11 (abstract + manuscript) — ~2 months out**
**Project: Plastic pathways (#2)**

**Who fits:**
- **Priya Raman (#6)** — closest profile match (62%), satellite oceanography
- **Mara Ellison (#4)** — 60% match
- **Jonah Whitcombe (#5)** — 59% match, marine litter and Lagrangian analysis

**Paper to strengthen the application:**
- **#39** — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea" (Rong et al., 2026). This is a strong methodological anchor for an IGARSS submission: it demonstrates a deep-learning pipeline for extracting ocean features from satellite imagery, which pairs naturally with a plastic-pathways paper that uses remote sensing to track or detect debris.
- **#32** — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter" (Lim & Hong, 2026) is the most directly relevant to the Plastic pathways project itself (particle-tracking, beaching, field validation), and would be the natural companion if the submission is about the pathway model rather than the detection method.

---

**Bottom line:** The ICGDA deadline is the one to move on this week. Priya is the strongest fit for both, but the #37 paper is the clearest hook for the heatwave project, and #39 is the clearest methodological hook for the plastic/remote-sensing project at IGARSS.

#36 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#39 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

final_text:
The paper that matters most for the Marine heatwave early warning project is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

**Why it stands out:**

1. **It's the only paper in the slate that demonstrates a full forecast-to-action loop for marine heatwaves.** The team used climate forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño to identify a high-risk MHW, convened an expert workshop, and triggered a pre-emptive rescue of 25 red handfish before the event hit. That's exactly the "early warning" architecture your project is building toward — a forecast that is credible enough to trigger a concrete response.

2. **It quantifies the stakes of getting the forecast right.** During the event, in-situ temperatures exceeded records for 80 days more than 2 °C above the long-term summer mean. Three of the 25 fish died in captivity; the rest were released after the MHW subsided with confirmed post-release survival. That's a real cost-benefit story for the value of early warning.

3. **It's a published, peer-reviewed precedent (2026) for proactive, forecast-triggered conservation in Australia** — the first of its kind for a protected marine species. That makes it a strong citation and a model for how your project's outputs could be operationalized with managers and stakeholders.

**Runners-up worth a look:**

- **#5** (Mojumder, 2026) evaluates 1–14-day ML forecasts of MHWs against persistence benchmarks in the Bay of Bengal. It's directly relevant to the ML-forecasting side of your project, but it's a thesis data release with a thin abstract, so the methodological detail is limited.
- **#3** (a comment on a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific) is useful for the seasonal-forecast and ecosystem-management angle, but it's a comment rather than the full system paper, and its focus is on a different region and timescale.

**Suggested next steps (in the app):**

- Save #4 to the project's reading list and note the forecast-trigger mechanism as a design reference.
- If you want to dig into the ML-forecasting method, request the full text of #5 or the underlying thesis.
- Consider adding #4's authors (Stuart-Smith, Hobday, Ling) to your lab's contact list if you'd like to discuss operationalizing forecast-triggered responses.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#10 [paper] Climatology of the sea temperature from long-term in situ observations: Northern Chilean Patagonia
Authors: Cécile Pujol, Alexander Barth, Iván Pérez‐Santos, Pamela Linford, Aïda Alvera Azcarate
Venue: Earth system science data
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-8167-2026
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for a high-resolution, four-dimensional temperature climatology for Northern Chilean Patagonia to provide reference conditions for detecting anomalies, assessing ecosystem functioning, and identifying long-term trends in a region with complex fjords and channels where satellite observation…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Reconstruction of temperature fields using the Data Interpolating Variational Analysis (DIVAnd) tool from approximately three million in situ observations collected over 75 years, producing monthly fields from the surface to 400 m depth with a horizontal resolution of about 900 m and over 32 vertic…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northern Chilean Patagonia, including specific features such as Reloncaví Sound, Comau and Puyuhuapi Fjords, Corcovado Gulf, and Ancud Gulf, based on in situ data collected over the past 75 years.
Abstract:
Abstract. Ocean climatologies are essential for understanding the mean state and variability of marine systems, providing reference conditions for detecting anomalies, assessing ecosystem functioning and identifying long-term trends. In this study, we present the first high-resolution, four-dimensional temperature climatology for Northern Chilean Patagonia, a region characterised by the presence of a complex network of fjords and channels. The climatology was generated from approximately three million in situ observations collected over the past 75 years from multiple datasets. Using the Data Interpolating Variational Analysis (DIVAnd) tool, temperature fields were reconstructed with a horizontal resolution of about 900 m and over 32 vertical levels, producing monthly fields from the surface to 400 m depth. The resulting climatology accurately reproduces the main spatial and seasonal temperature patterns reported in previous studies. Surface temperatures show strong summer gradients between the open Pacific and Northern Patagonia, while enclosed regions such as Reloncaví Sound, Comau and Puyuhuapi Fjords exhibit pronounced seasonal amplitude compared with the more stable Corcovado Gulf. Below surface, temperature gradients become smoother and the thermocline deepens in summer, typically ranging between 10 and 50 m. At 100 m depth, temperatures are relatively constant throughout the year, but spatial variations are still observed, with Ancud Gulf and Reloncaví Sound being slightly warmer. This climatology provides a refined and physically consistent representation of the oceanographic structure of Northern Patagonia, offering an essential baseline for future modelling, monitoring and climate-change assessments in a region where satellite observations are limited by persistent cloud cover and complex topography. All climatologies generated in this study are freely available online.

#3 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

#6 [paper] Data‐Driven Parameterization of Arctic Ocean Turbulent Mixing
Authors: Rafael Sebastian Reiss, Lisanne Blok, Nicholas Leonard, Kate Oglethorpe, Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, Colm-cille P. Caulfield, Ali Mashayek
Venue: Geophysical Research Letters
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1029/2026gl123721
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic Ocean turbulent mixing is poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding, despite its importance for regional dynamics and global overturning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Training gradient-boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data to predict turbulent dissipation from hydrographic variables, using spatial block cross-validation for evaluation.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles) for training; pan-Arctic hydrographic observations and high-resolution model output for application.
Abstract:
Abstract Turbulent mixing may become increasingly important in a changing Arctic Ocean, influencing regional dynamics and global overturning. Arctic turbulence remains poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding. We train gradient‐boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles; ∼ data points) to predict turbulent dissipation from more widely available hydrography. Global training is essential for skill across non‐Arctic and Arctic regions (, 75% within a factor of 2 of observations; = 0.47–0.55 under spatial block cross‐validation). Applied to pan‐Arctic hydrographic observations, predictions show enhanced dissipation along margins and shelves and weaker values in basin interiors, consistent with current understanding. Applied to high‐resolution model output, predictions reveal diffusivities and a basin‐integrated irreversible buoyancy flux consistent with observations, yet markedly different from the common K‐Profile Parameterization—with implications for simulated tracer transport. Our parameterization can help assess climate‐mixing feedbacks in projections while physics‐based parameterizations mature.

#7 [paper] Rescene-ESM: an Earth system model built around a frozen AI weather model
Authors: Minjong Cheon, Kaoru Kakinuma
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/e1c22d8441861158dd7f9e6021cb718096d3f29f
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The high computational cost of Earth system models limits the exploration of scenarios and ensemble members, while existing machine-learning weather models coupled to oceans have produced weak El Niño variability or relied on climate-model output, and none effectively routes climate impacts through…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model using a coupler named YAHO that links a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon, and energy components constrained by observations; the model uses an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave oc…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Simulations of approximately 1,000 years on one graphics processing unit; evaluation against observed climate data from 1979-2022; routing of runoff to 212 river gauges; and future projections for SSP1 and SSP3 scenarios for the period 2081-2100.
Abstract:
Earth system models underpin climate projections, but their cost limits how many scenarios, ensemble members and impact pathways can be explored. Machine-learning weather models forecast as skillfully as physics-based models at a fraction of the cost, yet coupled to an ocean they have produced weak El Nino variability or have learned it from climate-model output, and none carries the climate through rivers to the people exposed to it. Here we present Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model whose coupler, YAHO, yokes a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon and energy components constrained by observations. Adding the couplings one at a time shows what each contributes: over a climatological ocean the AI atmosphere varies from year to year by a third of the observed amount over the oceans, and an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave ocean, the residual of the observed sea surface temperature (SST) equation as stochastic forcing and the land's moisture flux raise this step by step and bring El Nino and its teleconnections, leaving the mean climate almost unchanged. The full model simulates about 1,000 years per day on one graphics processing unit, holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces the observed 1979-2022 global warming, carries forced change with a physically based structure around the frozen network (transient climate response 1.60 K), routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79 and, driven by emissions, separates the heatwave exposure of an SSP1 and an SSP3 world by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.

#9 [paper] FES2022 global tide atlas: a step towards SWOT-compliant tidal corrections
Authors: Florent Lyard, Loren Carrère, Ergane Fouchet, Mathilde Cancet, Ramiro Ferrari, Mei-Ling Dabat, Chafih Skandrani, David Greenberg
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-6805
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for high-resolution tidal corrections for modern altimetry missions like SWOT, specifically addressing residual issues in coastal, shelf, and polar areas that existed in the previous FES2014 model.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A hydrodynamic model (T-UGOm) using a tenfold increase in mesh resolution, a composite bathymetry dataset (GEBCO_2020 and regional patches) with a 2-meter depth threshold, regionally calibrated bottom friction and wave drag, atmospheric forcing from ERA5, and a two-iteration data assimilation proce…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean, with specific focus on coastal, shelf, and polar regions; validation performed using altimetry crossovers (Jason-3, AltiKa, Sentinel-3A), tide gauges, 119 current-meter stations, and GRACE gravity field residuals.
Abstract:
Abstract. The FES2022 Global Tide Atlas represents a significant advancement in global tidal modelling, specifically designed to meet the high-resolution tidal correction requirements of modern altimetry missions like the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission, which demand enhanced resolution and accuracy in the coastal seas. Building on the success of its predecessor FES2014, which performed well in most ocean regions but exhibited residuals issues in coastal, shelf, and polar areas, FES2022 introduces a tenfold increase in mesh resolution, prioritizing coastal and shelf regions. To some extent, this resolution aligns with SWOT’s KaRIn instrument capabilities, ensuring compatibility with its high-resolution ocean elevation measurements in shallow water regions. The bathymetry dataset is a composite of GEBCO_2020 and regional patches from other datasets, with a 2-meter depth threshold to better capture shallow coastal dynamics. The underlying hydrodynamic model (T-UGOm) includes both frequency-domain and time-stepping solvers, with the latter providing more accurate schemes for non-linearities in tides. Bottom friction and wave drag parameters were regionally calibrated. The model also incorporates atmospheric forcing from ERA5 to account for the radiational component of tides when relevant. The data assimilation process uses an ensemble Kalman filter with 358 members, generated by perturbing bathymetry, bottom friction, and wave drag. 16 tidal constituents were assimilated, along with 18 additional waves derived from time-stepping simulations. The assimilation was performed in two iterations (the second one resulting in the final FES2022b atlas) to incorporate the FES2022a Loading and Self-Attraction solution, enhancing the consistency between the model and the observations. The validation of FES2022b demonstrates substantial improvements over FES2014b and other state-of-the-art models. In the frequency domain, the Root Sum Square (RSS) errors for tidal elevations were reduced to 7.6 mm at altimetry crossovers in the deep ocean, 11.3 mm on shelves, and 42.3 mm at tide gauges compared to FES2014b. Temporal validation showed a variance reduction in Sea Surface Height (SSH) of -2.26 cm² for Jason-3 and -5.75 cm² for AltiKa when compared to FES2014b, with even greater reductions (-16.6 cm² for AltiKa) when compared to GOT4.10c. In polar regions, FES2022b significantly reduced the Sentinel-3A SSH variance in the Arctic (Baffin Bay, Siberian Shelf) and Antarctic (Ross and Weddell Seas). Coastal zones benefited from more than 40 cm² of variance reduction within 20 km of the shore. Tidal current validation using 119 current-meter stations showed a 56 % improvement compared to FES2014b, with a global RMSD of 2 cm/s for the major axis of tidal ellipses. GRACE gravity field residuals were also reduced, particularly around the Vancouver Island, from 10 cm to 3 cm EWE (Equivalent Water Elevation). Despite these advancements, some local residual errors persist due to bathymetry inaccuracies, shoreline misalignments, and limited high-latitude data coverage. These issues will be addressed in the future FES release. FES2022 is operational for altimetry de-aliasing corrections and available for download on the AVISO+ website, along with the prediction code on the CNES GitHub. Future improvements will focus on integrating latest bathymetry databases, refining shoreline databases, and enhancing high-latitude coverage of data assimilation through dedicated missions. The model’s unprecedented accuracy in coastal and polar regions makes it a recommended replacement for FES2014 in operational and scientific applications.

#12 [paper] Benchmark-based assessments of best-practice automatic quality control for ocean salinity in-situ observations
Authors: Zhetao Tan, Lijing Cheng, C. Coatanoan, Tanguy Szekely, Jérôme Gourrion, Zhankun Wang, James Reagan, Viktor Gouretski
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-6750
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of benchmark-based recommendations for automatic quality control (AutoQC) of ocean salinity in-situ observations, given the heterogeneous data quality in historical profile archives.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A benchmark-based approach under the International Quality-controlled Ocean Database (IQuOD) framework to compare suites of salinity AutoQC tests from seven international oceanographic institutions. The suites comprised 30 individual checks evaluated against manually quality-controlled benchmark da…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Historical ocean salinity profile archives and manually (expert) quality-controlled benchmark datasets from seven international oceanographic institutions.
Abstract:
Abstract. Ocean salinity is an Essential Ocean Variable that underpins our understanding of Earth’s climate system and the global hydrological cycle. Reliable and accurate salinity observations are therefore critical, yet historical profile archives contain heterogeneous data quality, and the community lacks benchmark-based recommendations for salinity automatic quality control (AutoQC). Under the International Quality-controlled Ocean Database (IQuOD) framework, we developed a benchmark-based approach to compare suites of salinity AutoQC tests from seven international oceanographic institutions. The suites comprised 30 individual checks and were evaluated based on several manually (expert) quality-controlled benchmark datasets. We assessed ~6,400 QC configurations in receiver operating characteristic (ROC) space and identified three best-practice schemes for distinct user priorities. These comprised a high-detection scheme with a high true-positive rate (HTPR), a conservative scheme with a low false-positive rate (LFPR), and a balanced scheme with a cut-off between HTPR and LFPR. We further examined their spatial and vertical performance and investigated factors underlying their contrasting behaviour, with local climatological range check and the constant-value checks accounted for most between-scheme differences. This result suggests that regional salinity structure, observational sampling density, and threshold design may strongly affect the trade-off between detecting erroneous observations and retaining valid data. Our results provide a transparent framework for salinity AutoQC best-practice recommendations while highlighting where an additional regional and depth-dependent validation remains necessary. The resulting schemes could support generating internally consistent QC flags for the first release of the IQuOD salinity database and, more broadly, could allow varying data centers and producers to select best-practice QC procedures for ocean reconstruction, modeling and operational oceanography, as well as allow the general data users to choose salinity QCed datasets flagged using the HTPR, LFPR, or Compromise schemes based on their research objectives and tolerance for potentially data errors.

final_text:
The clearest match for Plastic pathways is **#4 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it matters most:

- **It is the only item on the slate directly about marine litter.** The rest of the slate is about phytoplankton production (#3, #9), ocean forecast systems (#5), internal waves (#7), turtle telemetry (#12), and other remote-sensing topics — none of which touch debris pathways.
- **It is a methods paper, not just a result.** It provides a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, with the scripts that ran the particle-tracking experiments and the aggregated result files (#4). That is directly reusable infrastructure for modelling how plastic moves and where it ends up on shore.
- **It is validated against field records** from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories (#4) — a good template for the kind of field-anchored validation a pathways project needs.
- **It is open and current** (#4), and the underlying trajectories and flow fields are available on request, so the team could in principle reproduce or extend the experiments.

One caveat: the project's confirmed state (goals, blockers, milestones) is not visible to me in this conversation, so I cannot tie #4 to a specific open blocker. If the project has a blocker around beaching/stranding modelling or particle-tracking validation, #4 is the item to pull first.

Suggested next steps:
- Have Jonah or Priya read #4 and note whether the OceanParcels kernels fit the project's existing pipeline.
- If the project's state in the app is more than 30 days old, it may be worth re-confirming goals and blockers there so the slate can be tied to them more precisely.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Development and application of a tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter tracking.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A three-phase beaching kernel and six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, along with scripts for particle-tracking experiments and result aggregation.

Abstract:

Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, plus what's new and one funding angle.

## Where the project stands

I can see the project is a lab-scoped effort with three members: **Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you**. However, the confirmed state (goals, method, blockers, stage, milestones) came back empty — nothing has been recorded or confirmed in Mycelium for this project yet. So I can't tell you its stage or open blockers; if the team has been working on it, that context isn't captured here. You can fill that in via the app (project details in the project view).

## Three most relevant new papers

From the project's current slate, all entered this week:

1. **#7 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The most directly on-topic: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea using ROMS flow fields. If your project tracks where plastic goes, this is a ready-made method and codebase to build on or compare against.
2. **#12 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, *Remote Sensing*). Relevant on the methods side: a YOLO11-based detector for low-contrast, curved ocean features in satellite imagery. The same detection/segmentation approach could be adapted to spotting plastic debris or aggregation zones from space.
3. **#6 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model"** (Zhang, 2026, Zenodo). Relevant as the flow-field/forecast input side: daily analyses of a regional ocean forecast system, the kind of current and trajectory data you'd drive particle tracking with. (Note: Mycelium only holds the title and deposit details for this one — no abstract or method reading — so treat it as a lead to read rather than a summary I can vouch for.)

The other new slate items (#5 LiDAR phytoplankton, #9 a comment, #11 multi-object tracking) are further afield from plastic pathways.

## One funding opportunity

**#10 — NSF Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC)** — still open, deadline **15 February 2027**. It funds unsolicited proposals for instrumentation and technology development with broad applicability to ocean science. A natural fit: if Plastic pathways involves developing or adapting particle-tracking kernels, satellite-detection methods, or new observational tools for tracing debris, OTIC is built for exactly that kind of capability-building work.

A bigger, more collaborative alternative is **#3 — the EU's €50M call on strengthening the Global Ocean Observing System** (deadline 16 February 2027), which leans toward observing networks and biodiversity; it could work if the project frames debris observation as part of a broader ocean-observing contribution, but OTIC is the tighter single-project match.

**Suggested next steps:** read #7's code deposit to see how much you can reuse, and if the project's goals and blockers aren't yet recorded in Mycelium, capturing them in the app would let me tie future slate items to specific blockers.

#12 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#32 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#33 [paper] A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period.
Authors: Zhenhua Zhang, Peng Chen, Siqi Zhang, Delu Pan
Venue: Science Advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aej4633
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The authors used 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP). A bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions, and low-light estimates were generated as physically const…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Arctic region, specifically marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions, using spaceborne LiDAR data from 2006 to 2023.
Abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year −1 during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.
