Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

#38 [paper] Data‐Driven Parameterization of Arctic Ocean Turbulent Mixing
Authors: Rafael Sebastian Reiss, Lisanne Blok, Nicholas Leonard, Kate Oglethorpe, Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, Colm-cille P. Caulfield, Ali Mashayek
Venue: Geophysical Research Letters
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1029/2026gl123721
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic Ocean turbulent mixing is poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding, despite its importance for regional dynamics and global overturning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Training gradient-boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data to predict turbulent dissipation from hydrographic variables, using spatial block cross-validation for evaluation.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles) for training; pan-Arctic hydrographic observations and high-resolution model output for application.
Abstract:
Abstract Turbulent mixing may become increasingly important in a changing Arctic Ocean, influencing regional dynamics and global overturning. Arctic turbulence remains poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding. We train gradient‐boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles; ∼ data points) to predict turbulent dissipation from more widely available hydrography. Global training is essential for skill across non‐Arctic and Arctic regions (, 75% within a factor of 2 of observations; = 0.47–0.55 under spatial block cross‐validation). Applied to pan‐Arctic hydrographic observations, predictions show enhanced dissipation along margins and shelves and weaker values in basin interiors, consistent with current understanding. Applied to high‐resolution model output, predictions reveal diffusivities and a basin‐integrated irreversible buoyancy flux consistent with observations, yet markedly different from the common K‐Profile Parameterization—with implications for simulated tracer transport. Our parameterization can help assess climate‐mixing feedbacks in projections while physics‐based parameterizations mature.

#39 [paper] Rescene-ESM: an Earth system model built around a frozen AI weather model
Authors: Minjong Cheon, Kaoru Kakinuma
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/e1c22d8441861158dd7f9e6021cb718096d3f29f
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The high computational cost of Earth system models limits the exploration of scenarios and ensemble members, while existing machine-learning weather models coupled to oceans have produced weak El Niño variability or relied on climate-model output, and none effectively routes climate impacts through…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model using a coupler named YAHO that links a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon, and energy components constrained by observations; the model uses an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave oc…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Simulations of approximately 1,000 years on one graphics processing unit; evaluation against observed climate data from 1979-2022; routing of runoff to 212 river gauges; and future projections for SSP1 and SSP3 scenarios for the period 2081-2100.
Abstract:
Earth system models underpin climate projections, but their cost limits how many scenarios, ensemble members and impact pathways can be explored. Machine-learning weather models forecast as skillfully as physics-based models at a fraction of the cost, yet coupled to an ocean they have produced weak El Nino variability or have learned it from climate-model output, and none carries the climate through rivers to the people exposed to it. Here we present Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model whose coupler, YAHO, yokes a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon and energy components constrained by observations. Adding the couplings one at a time shows what each contributes: over a climatological ocean the AI atmosphere varies from year to year by a third of the observed amount over the oceans, and an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave ocean, the residual of the observed sea surface temperature (SST) equation as stochastic forcing and the land's moisture flux raise this step by step and bring El Nino and its teleconnections, leaving the mean climate almost unchanged. The full model simulates about 1,000 years per day on one graphics processing unit, holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces the observed 1979-2022 global warming, carries forced change with a physically based structure around the frozen network (transient climate response 1.60 K), routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79 and, driven by emissions, separates the heatwave exposure of an SSP1 and an SSP3 world by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.

#41 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

final_text:
The one that matters most is **#5 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

Why it stands out for this project:

- **It's the closest thing to a working example of your project's end goal.** Your project is about *early warning* — and this paper documents a case where a climate forecast ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño flagged a high-risk marine heatwave, an expert workshop judged it a severe threat, and that judgment triggered a real, pre-emptive rescue of a Critically Endangered species before the heatwave hit. That's the full loop you're trying to build: forecast → risk assessment → action, with the action landing *before* the extreme.
- **It shows the decision-making layer, not just the forecast.** Most of the other papers in the feed are about the forecasting machinery itself. #5 is about what happens *after* a forecast — how experts and institutions turned a predicted extreme into a concrete, approved intervention (25 fish captured in January 2024, held through a period of 80 days more than 2°C above the long-term mean summer temperature, then released with post-release survival confirmed). For an early-warning project, that governance and response side is exactly the part that's hard to design.
- **It's a cautionary benchmark too.** Three fish died in captivity, and the whole exercise needed commonwealth, state and institutional approvals — useful evidence of the practical and ethical constraints your warning system will have to anticipate.

The runner-up is **#6** (Mojumder, 2026), which is the most directly on-topic methodologically — it evaluates 1–14-day machine-learning MHW forecasts against persistence benchmarks, which speaks straight to your ML data-assimilation interests. But it's a B.S. thesis data release from Zenodo, so it's a useful reference point for benchmarking rather than a source of design insight. #5 gives you the "why and how of acting on a forecast" that #6 can't.

#5 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

The clear standout is **#7 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it matters most for Plastic pathways:

- **It's the only item on the slate that is directly about marine litter.** The others touch the project at best indirectly: #6 is a data-assimilation product for a Pacific forecast system, #12 is satellite detection of internal waves, #5 is Arctic phytoplankton, #9 is a seasonal ocean forecast, and #11 is a computer-vision tracking paper.
- **It addresses the "last mile" of a pathways study.** The paper develops a three-phase beaching kernel (plus six other particle kernels) for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories (#7). That's exactly the kind of transport-to-shore component a pathways project needs to close the loop between open-ocean drift and where debris actually ends up.
- **It's immediately usable.** The deposit includes the kernel code, the experiment scripts, the aggregated results behind every number in the manuscript, and a reproduction manifest (#7). The raw trajectories (~32 GB) and ROMS flow fields (~37 GB) are available on request. That means Jonah, Priya or you could adapt the kernel to your own domain rather than re-deriving it.

One caveat: the project's confirmed state isn't visible to me right now, so I can't tie this to a specific open blocker — but on the slate as it stands, #7 is the item the team should read first. If you'd like, I can pull up the full text of the underlying manuscript or dig into how the kernel is parameterized.

#12 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#5 [paper] A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period.
Authors: Zhenhua Zhang, Peng Chen, Siqi Zhang, Delu Pan
Venue: Science Advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aej4633
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The authors used 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP). A bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions, and low-light estimates were generated as physically const…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Arctic region, specifically marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions, using spaceborne LiDAR data from 2006 to 2023.
Abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year −1 during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

Both grants are still open, so the comparison is live. Here's how they line up against the Marine heatwave early warning project (#3).

**#1 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS)**
- €50M, deadline 16 Feb 2027.
- Aims: strengthen and operationalise the global observing network — deploying equipment, observing system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), network optimisation, technology roadmaps with industry — with a focus on areas beyond national jurisdiction, polar regions, the deep sea, and biodiversity observations, all under the IOC-GOOS / Copernicus framework.
- Fit with #3: this is the closer match. An early-warning project for marine heatwaves lives on exactly the kind of thing this call funds — sustained, fit-for-purpose ocean observations and the data delivery behind them. The call's emphasis on "reliable services" and closing structural gaps in under-observed regions is where a heatwave forecasting effort would naturally slot in: better observations, better assimilation, earlier warning. The main doubt is that the call is heavily framed around infrastructure, governance and biodiversity, so the proposal would need to be written as an observing-systems contribution rather than a pure forecasting-methods project.

**#2 — A safe operating space for Antarctica and the Southern Ocean**
- €5–11M, deadline 23 Sep 2027.
- Aims: resolve uncertainties and improve near-, mid- and long-term projections for the Antarctic and Southern Ocean — ocean–atmosphere–sea-ice–ice-sheet interactions, tipping points, ecosystem vulnerability, monitoring indicators — with a specific focus on Antarctic continental shelves and bottom-water formation regions.
- Fit with #3: weaker. It does touch extreme events, but only as part of a much broader Earth-system projection agenda centred on Antarctica and the cryosphere. Unless the heatwork project has a strong Southern Ocean / Antarctic component, this call is aimed at a different region and a different question (decadal-to-millennial projections and tipping points, not operational early warning).

**Bottom line:** #1 fits the Marine heatwave early warning project better — its core is building the observing and data-delivery capacity that an early-warning system depends on, whereas #2 is a region-specific, long-horizon projection call centred on Antarctica. The biggest doubt on #1 is that it is infrastructure- and governance-heavy, so the application would need to be framed around observing-systems contribution rather than forecasting methods alone.

One honest caveat: I could only see the project's name and members (#3) — its detailed state (problem statement, method, milestones) was not available to me in this conversation, so this comparison is based on the project's declared focus (marine heatwave prediction, sea surface temperature forecasting) rather than its full internal description. If you'd like, I can also check who in the lab would be the strongest lead author for either call.

# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

Now I have a comprehensive picture. Let me synthesize everything into a clear answer.

Here's what I found, Mara:

---

## Best-fitting open grant: #15 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System" (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)

This is the clear winner over #10 (NSF OTIC, deadline 2027-02-15). Here's why:

**Why #15 fits the Marine heatwave early warning project:**
- The project's core concepts — marine heatwave prediction, ocean data assimilation, subseasonal forecasting, sea surface temperature — map directly onto the grant's focus on strengthening the GOOS, improving observing system outputs, and providing reliable climate and biodiversity services.
- The grant explicitly calls for "data delivery that is fit-for-purpose, cost efficient and designed across all its components" — which is exactly what a marine heatwave early warning system delivers: operational, actionable forecasts from assimilated observations.
- The project's data assimilation work (your declared strength) is a natural contribution to the grant's emphasis on "strengthened and resilient global ocean observing capacities."
- The €50M scale and Horizon Europe framing mean there's room for a multi-partner consortium, which is where the external partnerships come in.

**Why #10 is a weaker fit:**
- NSF OTIC is specifically about *instrumentation development* — new hardware, sensors, analytical tools. The Marine heatwave early warning project is about *forecasting and data assimilation methodology*, not building new instruments. None of the lab's declared profiles cover instrumentation development, and the nightly ranking only found weak profile matches (62–65%) for Tomás, Sun-hee, and Jonah.

---

## Who in the lab should lead

**You (Mara Ellison) should lead the application.** Here's the evidence:

- **You cover the grant's central requirement** — "stabilise, further strengthen and operationalise the global ocean observing system" — with your declared expertise in ocean data assimilation. The nightly ranking named you as a top fit, noting that "your integration of data assimilation with machine learning for ocean forecasting enhances the resilience and accuracy of the observing system's outputs."
- **You're the PI and project owner** of the Marine heatwave early warning project, so you have the institutional authority and the deepest context on the project's goals, methods, and gaps.
- **Priya Raman (#4)** is the strongest co-lead or co-PI. She covers the same central requirement through her declared expertise in satellite ocean remote sensing, and the ranking noted that "your use of satellite ocean colour remote sensing to map water quality contributes to the strengthened global ocean observing capacities and data coordination." Satellite observations are a key input to any GOOS-strengthening proposal, and her coastal water quality background adds the biodiversity/ecosystem angle the grant asks for.

**Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#6)** is a strong supporting voice for the physics-informed ML and data assimilation methodology sections, given his declared interests in circulation/turbulence and physics-informed ML.

**Sun-hee Park (#5)** could contribute on the operational data tools and dashboard side — the project's "ocean data dashboards" concept is one of the gaps no member currently declares, and her declared interest in ocean data tools is the closest match.

**Gaps to address in the team:**
- No one in the lab declares expertise in **observing system experiments (OSEs)**, **observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs)**, or **network optimisation approaches** — all explicitly called for by the grant.
- No one covers **areas beyond national jurisdiction** (ABNJ), which the grant emphasises.
- The grant asks for **industry partners** (SMEs, technology providers, maritime industries, service operators) — a role no lab member is matched to.

These gaps are exactly where external partners come in.

---

## Who outside the lab could partner

Based on the papers on the project's slate and their author teams, here are the most natural external partners:

1. **Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang** (authors of #20, "Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation") — They're building a 40-day global MHW forecast framework with end-to-end neural assimilation, which is directly complementary to your project's data assimilation + MHW prediction focus. Their work on mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction in a dynamic kernel is a strong methodological partner for the "strengthen observing system outputs" angle.

2. **Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong** (authors of #23, "Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture") — They've demonstrated a 38-hour mean advisory lead time for operational MHW early warning in a real aquaculture setting. This is exactly the "fit-for-purpose data delivery" and "reliable services" outcome the grant asks for, and their South Korean operational context adds geographic diversity to the consortium.

3. **Gregory C. Smith, Fabrice Hernández, Charly Régnier, and the OceanPredict Intercomparison and Validation Task Team** (authors of #24, "Near Real-time Evaluation of Operational Oceanographic Predictions") — They've run a decade-long intercomparison of operational ocean forecasts, which is directly relevant to the grant's emphasis on "validation, procurement readiness, uptake and large-scale deployment of innovative ocean observing technologies." Their work on multi-system spread and uncertainty is a natural fit for the OSSE/evaluation component that's a gap in your lab.

4. **Yanzhi Zhou, Zipeng Yu, Tao Zhang, and the LICOM team** (authors of #27, "LFS-SEnDA: a global ocean forecast system with an efficient Sliding-Ensemble-based Data Assimilation scheme") — Their SEnDA scheme achieves a 30-fold speedup in the analysis step and ranks among leading global ocean forecast systems. This is a strong methodological partner for the data assimilation efficiency angle, and their work in the IV-TT Class-4 assessment framework connects to the operational verification community.

5. **Simone Spada, Anna Teruzzi, Stefano Maset, and the Venice team** (authors of #28, "GHOSH filter for computationally efficient data assimilation") — They've demonstrated a higher-order ensemble DA filter applied to satellite chlorophyll assimilation in a Mediterranean physical-biogeochemical model, with direct relevance to Copernicus Marine Service operational settings. This bridges the data assimilation and biodiversity observation angles the grant asks for.

**Note on introduction paths:** None of these external authors are in Mycelium's graph, so I can't trace co-authorship chains or existing connections to you. You'd need to reach out directly — the papers are all 2026 publications, so the teams are active and likely open to collaboration.

---

**Summary:** Apply to #15 (Horizon Europe GOOS, €50M, deadline 2027-02-16). You lead, Priya co-leads, Tomás and Sun-hee support. Partner with the Ocean-E2E team (Shu et al.), the South Korean aquaculture MHW team (Kang et al.), the OceanPredict intercomparison team (Smith et al.), and the LICOM/SEnDA team (Zhou et al.) to fill the gaps in OSE/OSSE, ABNJ, and industry.

#20 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

#23 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

#24 [paper] Near Real-time Evaluation of Operational Oceanographic Predictions: Over a Decade of Intercomparison by Global Ocean Forecasting Centers
Authors: Gregory C. Smith, Fabrice Hernández, Charly Régnier, Saima Aijaz, Alain Caya, Ric Crocker, Marie Drévillon, Yvonnick Le Clainche
Venue: Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1175/bams-d-25-0185.1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for near real-time evaluation of operational oceanographic predictions to ensure consistency, quality, and understanding of multi-system spread and uncertainty.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Intercomparison of operational analyses and forecasts against common observational datasets.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A decade-long intercomparison project under the OceanPredict Intercomparison and Validation Task Team, including sea ice concentration and 15-m currents datasets.
Abstract:
Abstract Near real-time evaluations of operational predictions are required to ensure consistency and quality of forecasts. When possible, intercomparisons of such predictions against common observational datasets allows a further understanding of multi-system spread and uncertainty in predictions, and sheds light on quality of both numerical prediction and observational datasets. For the physical ocean, an intercomparison of operational analyses and forecasts was put in place in 2012 under the auspices of the OceanPredict Intercomparison and Validation Task Team. With over a decade of experience demonstrating the evolution of the accuracy of operational oceanographic predictions, this valuable dataset provides a community resource to underpin additional studies such as the benchmarking of deep-learning neural-network emulators. Here we highlight the lessons learned and challenges encountered in this activity and describe how the system is evolving from a research effort into an operational verification activity. We also describe two additional datasets that have been added, namely, sea ice concentration and 15-m currents.

#11 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#27 [paper] LFS-SEnDA: a global ocean forecast system with an efficient Sliding-Ensemble-based Data Assimilation scheme
Authors: Yanzhi Zhou, Zipeng Yu, Tao Zhang, Jiangfeng Yu, Maoxue Yu, Kai Xu, Weipeng Zheng, Hailong Liu
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-4602
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Improving computational efficiency and analysis quality in global ocean data assimilation, particularly in eddy-rich regions, compared to conventional Ensemble Optimal Interpolation.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of the Sliding-Ensemble-based Data Assimilation (SEnDA) scheme, which uses time-dependent sliding ensemble samples to represent temporally varying background-error covariance structures, incorporates a parallel-friendly analysis procedure, and employs an accelerated solver.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The LICOM Forecast System, evaluated within the IV-TT Class-4 assessment framework for global ocean forecasting.
Abstract:
Abstract. This study develops an efficient Sliding-Ensemble-based Data Assimilation (SEnDA) scheme and integrates it into the LICOM Forecast System to establish LFS-SEnDA. In SEnDA, time-dependent sliding ensemble samples are used to represent temporally varying background-error covariance structures. Meanwhile, SEnDA has incorporated a parallel-friendly analysis procedure and an accelerated solver to improve computational efficiency. Compared with the conventional Ensemble Optimal Interpolation scheme, SEnDA improves analysis quality, particularly in eddy-rich regions, and achieves about a 30-fold speedup in analysis step. Within the IV-TT Class-4 assessment, LFS-SEnDA ranks among the leading candidate global ocean forecast systems and achieves the highest composite score based on sea surface temperature, sea level anomaly, upper-ocean temperature, and salinity over forecast days 1–6. At a 1-day lead time, LFS-SEnDA achieves global RMSEs of approximately 0.38 °C for sea surface temperature and 0.06 m for sea level anomaly. These results indicate that LFS-SEnDA provides an efficient and scalable framework for improving multi-variate ocean state estimation and global ocean forecasting.

#28 [paper] A novel Gauss-Hermite High-Order Sampling Hybrid ensemble filter for computationally efficient data assimilation in geosciences – Part 2: OGSTM-BFM-GHOSH
Authors: Simone Spada, Anna Teruzzi, Stefano Maset, Stefano Salon, Cosimo Solidoro, Gianpiero Cossarini
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-3182
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract. Data assimilation (DA) methodologies play a crucial role in integrating observational data with numerical models to provide accurate state estimates of geophysical systems. A novel ensemble algorithm, the Gauss-Hermite High-Order Sampling Hybrid (GHOSH) filter, aims to improve DA performances by featuring an approximation order higher than in other ensemble DA filters like SEIK (Singular Evolutive Interpolated Kalman filter) or ETKF (Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter). Building upon the successful application in idealized twin experiments (Part 1), we propose a parallel implementation of the GHOSH filter which has been coupled with a realistic geophysical application: the assimilation of surface satellite chlorophyll in a physical-biogeochemical model of the Mediterranean Sea (OGSTM-BFM). This application was selected due to its complexity and potential relevance to operational settings, such as those of the Copernicus Marine Service, where the uncertainty of prediction can also be crucial. By assimilating satellite chlorophyll data, GHOSH aims to improve the accuracy of the state estimation, not only for the assimilated variable but also for other non-assimilated variables of interest (nutrients), thereby enhancing our understanding of marine ecosystem dynamics. The simulation results are validated using both semi-independent (satellite chlorophyll) and independent (nutrient concentrations from an in-situ climatology) observations. Results show that: i) the GHOSH implementation in a realistic three-dimensional application is just as computationally feasible as other ensemble assimilation filters, since the integration of a realistic model is by far more computationally expensive than the assimilation scheme; ii) the GHOSH assimilation algorithm improved the agreement between forecasts and observations without producing unrealistic effects on the non-assimilated variables. Moreover, a sensitivity analysis revealed correlation between higher order and a key nutrient (nitrate) estimation improvement, highlighting the importance of the GHOSH enhanced order of approximation in boosting DA performances on non-assimilated variables.

Here's what I found.

## Best fit: #12 — ZEWT Partnership (waterborne transport & marine ecosystems)

Of the open grants I could see, #12 is the closest to the Plastic pathways project. It's about evaluating, modelling, and mitigating pollution sources in European marine waters — €2M–€13.5M, deadline **14 April 2027**. The overlap is in the marine-pollution-modelling and forecasting side of your work.

The biggest doubt: the call is specifically about **renewable low- and zero-carbon fuels** (spills, operations, abatement systems at TRL 5). If Plastic pathways is about plastic debris pathways rather than fuel-related pollution, the fit is partial — you'd be pitching the modelling and environmental-impact side, not the fuel technology.

The other open grants I checked are further away:
- **#6** (Microplastics Research & Resource Coordination Center, deadline 1 Dec 2026) is about biomedical health effects and lab standardization — a different community.
- **#15** (Green, circular and resilient harbours, deadline 21 Sep 2027) is port-management and place-based action, needing port authorities in 4 basins.
- **#14** (Global Ocean Observing System, €50M, deadline 16 Feb 2027) is about observing infrastructure, not pollution pathways.

## Who in the lab should lead

I checked the lab's declared profiles against each call. No one's declared interests cover the specific requirement slots of #12 (waterborne-transport impacts, ports, Copernicus/EGNOS). The nightly ranking puts:

1. **Priya Raman** — closest profile match (67%), with declared interests in satellite oceanography and coastal water quality
2. **Jonah Whitcombe** — 64%, declared interests in marine litter and Lagrangian analysis
3. **Sun-hee Park** — 62%, declared interests in ocean data tools

Jonah's declared marine-litter and Lagrangian-analysis interests are the most directly on-topic for a plastic-pathways proposal, so he's the natural lead for the science core, with Priya covering the water-quality/monitoring angle. You'd be PI as usual.

## Partners outside the lab

I can't see any: collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so no outside suggestions are available to me. What I can say from the call itself is that #12 explicitly asks for **environmental, industry, and academic associations** in the consortium — so a port or shipping industry partner and an environmental NGO would be the natural additions to seek. You'd need to find them through your own networks.

One thing I couldn't check: the full eligibility rules of #12 (institution type, consortium size, country requirements) aren't in what I could read, so it's worth confirming those before committing.

results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

Amount: €2,000,000–€13,500,000

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The decarbonization of waterborne transport using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels introduces new, unexplored risks to marine and aquatic ecosystems, including pollution from normal operations and accidental spills, threatening the achievement of Good Environmental and Ecological Status in Europ…
Method (Mycelium's reading): The project aims to evaluate and forecast environmental impacts, model pollution sources, and develop, demonstrate, and test innovative prevention, abatement, and mitigation systems and strategies (targeting TRL 5) for managing spills and reducing harmful impacts of zero-emission fuels.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European marine waters, inland waterways, and port areas, focusing on waterborne transport operations using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes.

- Improved water resilience and good environmental and good ecological status in European waters and contribute to the achievement of the European Union's environmental targets, including the European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact.

- A comprehensive understanding of the future environmental impacts of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, addressing in particular pollution sources from: i) navigation on renewable low and zero-carbon fuels; and ii) accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels for marine waters, inland waters and ports (water and air quality).

- Innovative prevention, abatement and mitigation systems and strategies for reducing and eliminating the harmful impacts of waterborne transport on waters.

- Enhanced pollution prevention and mitigation in marine waters, inland waterways and port areas, reducing the likelihood and impact of accidents involving renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.

Scope:

The European Union aims to protect and conserve its marine and freshwater environments by achieving Good Environmental and Good Ecological Status[1]. The European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact further emphasize the need to enhance the resilience of European waters to human-induced pressures. Projects like the Horizon Europe EMERGE have researched the impacts of shipping on marine ecosystems. The introduction of technologies to decarbonize the sector may enable, to a certain extent, to phase-out relevant current sources of water and air pollution. However, renewable low and zero-carbon fuels and procedures pose new risks to marine and other aquatic ecosystems like rivers and lakes yet to be explored and addressed, both from the normal function of waterborne transport[2] and from accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels. In addition, other pollution sources can be addressed today[3]. This topic aims to evaluate, forecast, control and mitigate the impact of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, with a focus on developing and demonstrating innovative abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to mitigate and eliminate, where possible, the harmful impact of waterborne transport in the ocean and inland waters. New technologies and solutions addressing the decarbonization of waterborne transport will be considered, as well as the potential risks and challenges associated with these.

Actions should address all of the following aspects:

- Evaluate and forecast the environmental impacts of waterborne transport operations on marine, rivers and other aquatic ecosystems, in particular regarding the effects of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels (with particular attention to accidental spills) and related technologies. The proposal may include testing and experimental work in relation with spills.

- Develop and demonstrate effective response scenarios, including the associated abatement technologies and any potential new innovative equipment, for managing uncontrolled releases of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels in marine and inland waters or in port areas, including dedicated specific procedures and operational guidelines.

- Modelling scenarios on water and air pollution sources from each ship types and services running on renewable low and zero carbon fuels.

- Develop and demonstrate innovative and cost-effective abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to prevent, eliminate and reduce the harmful impacts of the use of renewable low and zero carbon fuels. Relevant TRL5 demonstration of such systems should be done.

- Identifying training needs and skills requirements to deploy developed solutions, as well as in relation to the management and use of renewable low carbon fuels in ports and on vessels in marine and inland waters, including relevant emergency response preparedness.

Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-CIRCBIO-03
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-22
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- environment and society at large benefit from recyclable plastic products which can be recycled back into high value applications;

- industrial value chains introduce circular plastic products on the market through enhanced design for recycling and solutions for effective sorting and recycling on a large scale;

- industrial value chains are equipped with improved characterisation of waste from complex plastic materials to enable its recycling.

Scope:

The topic supports the European Green Deal, the Regulation on Packaging and Packaging Waste, the Waste Shipment Regulation, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and its working plan, the upcoming Circular Economy Act and contributes to Europe’s efforts to develop a single market for sustainable products. It also contributes to the new EU bioeconomy strategy, the Life Sciences Strategy and the EU Biotech Act and is relevant to the European Commission’s communication: ‘Building the future with nature: Boosting Biotechnology and Biomanufacturing in the EU’.

Proposals should:

- advance novel biotech solutions for recycling of complex plastic materials and products (multi-material/multi-layer/composites), namely in the sectors of packaging, construction, renewable energy infrastructure and transport;

- propose recommendations towards fit-for-purpose regulatory risk assessments for novel materials and recycling technologies (i.e. hazard identification, methodological updates) and take into account the Safe-and-Sustainable-by-Design framework;

- consider the latest solutions in material innovation while developing novel recycling solutions e.g. by application of microbes and enzymes for enhanced degradation of plastics;

- demonstrate the solutions on a pilot scale involving the whole value chain.

Successful proposals are expected to evaluate the feasibility, effectiveness and impact of the demonstrated solutions using robust evaluation methods (including lifecycle assessments such as product environmental footprint, where relevant) and present data and evidence about the economic, environmental and social costs and benefits of the developed solutions.

Industrial value chains are expected to take part in the proposed consortia to enable a demonstration of the proposed solution and involve all relevant stakeholders.

Clustering with other relevant Horizon Europe projects is encouraged.

Technology Readiness Level - Technology readiness level expected from completed projects

Activities are expected to achieve TRL 4-5 by the end of the project – see General Annex B. Activities may start at any TRL.

Method (Mycelium's reading): Strengthening the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) through the deployment of observation equipment, performing observing system experiments (OSEs) and observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs), applying network optimization approaches, co-creating technology roadmaps with industry, and in…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean observing frameworks, specifically the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS), areas beyond national jurisdiction, and the Copernicus Marine Service.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Proposals are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes, in full alignment with the OceanEye initiative:

- scientists, public authorities and businesses benefit from strengthened and resilient global ocean observing capacities, coordinated under the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS),[1] through the deployment of ocean observation equipment, in particular for the provision of critical observations for marine biodiversity and ecosystem knowledge;

- public authorities prioritise investments on infrastructures and capacity building to advance ocean research, protect and restore ocean health and biodiversity and provide critical services through a global ocean observing system and data delivery that is fit-for purpose, cost efficient and designed across all its components;

- increased EU leadership and strategic autonomy in global ocean observation capabilities, in support of EU climate and biodiversity goals, strengthening the EU’s contribution to and influence within GOOS, and reducing the risk of critical dependencies, notably for key services (i.e. Copernicus Services);

- enhanced collaboration between observation communities, marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators, actionably contributing to the validation, procurement readiness, uptake and large-scale deployment of innovative ocean observing technologies and approaches, in particular for biodiversity observations, while reinforcing the long-term sustainability of the global ocean observing system.

Achieving these objectives requires sustained, global, interoperable and open ocean observations, as well as the knowledge and the capacity to use these observations.

IOC-GOOS, constituting the internationally recognised framework for in situ ocean observations worldwide, provides the global backbone for the development and monitoring of Essential Ocean Variables (EOVs),[2] and underpins European capacities such as Copernicus Marine Service and EU-funded research and innovation activities under Horizon Europe. Sustained and resilient ocean observation is crucial for marine biodiversity conservation and restoration under a changing climate, meaning that maintaining an optimised global ocean observing system is very important to achieve biodiversity goals.
